Mark Arnold writes speculative fiction with a broken remote in one hand and a sociology paper in the other.

Issued by the Unified Earth Government, Office of Cosmic Silence

Following the Cascade Incident, the Yarrow Misunderstanding and what is now formally called The Cake Problem, these protocols have been aggressively revised. Read carefully. Your late predecessors did not.

Nothing. All unknown alien lifeforms are extremely dangerous, and death is the usual First Contact result — for the human. Most personnel therefore prefer attending the Second Contact proceedings.

Suddenly remember you have an important appointment on the other side of the Galaxy. Do not answer. You are a rock. If you must answer, say “I am a rock.”

Ask them to state the nature of their emergency. If no emergency, put them on HOLD.

“It’s complicated.” “Around.” Never name a location you would like to keep. You are from nowhere. Continue this trend. Geography is a vulnerability. Wave in a vague direction and mumble, “Over thereabouts …”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Friendliness is a hunting strategy. Your cat is friendly. The alien’s dead bird on the doorstep will be you.

Do not listen to your Engineers. They will say it would be cool. It isn’t.

The first alien species we ever contacted bred by laying eggs in your chest. Bring protection. Flamethrowers are kept in Storage B12.

Nothing good responds instantly. Delay your reply. Aim for disinterest, not malfunction. You are busy doing nothing elsewhere. Maintain that illusion.

You will. That’s how we lost Star Base 2.

No. You are, if a member of the Core, body count. Be a version that could belong anywhere and nowhere at the same time.

They will not define ‘this’. Do not ask. Undefined ‘this’ cannot be repeated and cannot be tracked. Leave it unresolved. Agree but do not fix a specific date. Do not, under any excuse, use the word ‘date’.

Decline. Do not swallow alien embryos. They taste of regret.

Quarantine. Two weeks minimum. Do not assume the thing wearing their face remembers your birthday.

No. Ask about their breathing requirements. Then say, “Oh, sorry, we don’t breathe that,” and change the subject immediately. Do not revisit the topic.

They are always the last of their kind. The last of its kind has a lot of free time and a lot of anger. Do not become its hobby.

You will. Internalize it. You have practice. Panic is normal. Displaying it is optional and discouraged. Don’t be a target.

You are still breathing and they do not know where the rest of us are. That is considered a success under current guidelines. Survival is the only metric.

#1043. Who will replace Pierre Sage at Crystal Palace? Odds suspended on Thomas Frank

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The former Tottenham and Brentford boss is the favourite to take over the Eagles

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Pierre Sage became the second managerial casualty of the Premier League season as the former Crystal Palace manager was sacked mere hours after Manchester United had removed Michael Carrick from his position.

His departure is unsurprising given Palace’s position at the bottom of the table and the Frenchman has left the club following a fourth successive defeat.

Sage made the switch to Selhurst Park in the summer to replace Oliver Glasner - who has since moved to Nottingham Forest - and he signed a three-year contract.

He lasted just 16 games in all competitions at Palace and claimed just seven points out of a possible 30 during his tenure,

The search is now on for his replacement ahead of Palace’s next fixture on Saturday 21 November where they will come up against Frank Lampard’s Coventry City.

The current, overwhelming favourite to take up the head coach role is former Tottenham and Brentford boss Thomas Frank with betting sites having suspended betting on him. Frank was the 1/4 favourite to replace Sage before the axe fell on the former Eagles boss and his appointment at Selhurst Park would end an eight month exile from the top-flight after Frank was sacked by Spurs back in February.

Frank has been out of work since his early departure from Spurs but his previous role at Brentford is proof of his credentials and a possible snapshot of what he could achieve with Palace.

However, in taking on the role Frank will firstly need to deal with a relegation battle and ensure the club remains in the Premier League. Palace sold several key players last summer including Maxence Lacroix, Brennan Johnson, and Daniel Munoz while star men Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr have been struck with injuries.

Palace are yet to make a decision on their next manager, though all signs point to Frank, but former Burnley and Everton manager Sean Dyche is also in the running with betting sites giving him odds of 6/1 to replace Sage.

Dyche certainly has pedigree when it comes to avoiding relegation having kept Burnley in the top-flight from 2016 until his sacking in 2022 and avoiding the drop with Everton in 2023. Dyche would perhaps be a short term option for the Eagles but he would also be a future-proof one having twice lifted Burnley out of the Championship and into the Premier League.

Danish manager Jens Berthel Askou has reportedly emerged as a candidate for the Crystal Palace job with bookmakers offering a 6/1 chance for him to replace Sage as well.

After a season in charge of Motherwell, Askou moved to Toulouse and has since made a steady start to life in French football, with his team sitting 12th in Ligue 1 after collecting 13 points from their opening 10 matches.

His side have recorded three victories, four draws and three defeats, scoring 15 goals and conceding 14.

Askou has caught the eye of Crystal Palace’s decision makers but his appointment would be a riskier option considering managers are available with previous Premier League experience.

Other possible choices are Tony Popovic at 7/1, while Vitor Pereira and Vitor Matos both sit at 12/1 on betting sites.

#1042. The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.

This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.

But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.

While the other regional champions in the German fourth division were promoted to the nationwide 3. Liga, "Lok" faced a play-off against a representative of the Regional League Bavaria, Wurzburger Kickers. Ziane scored, but an injury-ravaged Leipzig lost 3-1 on aggregate.

"Euer System ist krank," read a simple protest banner displayed by the 2,000 travelling supporters â "your system is sick".

"It's the worst thing â injury aside â that you can experience as a footballer," Ziane tells BBC Sport.

"Catastrophe doesn't cut it. It doesn't make any sense. If they really wanted to change it, they could do tomorrow."

A banner reading 'Your system is sick' was displayed at this year's promotion play-off

Germany's football pyramid has a bottleneck.

Beneath the Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga, the fourth tier is split into five regional divisions (North, West, Southwest, Northeast and Bavaria), each of which produces a league champion.

So far, so good. But with only four teams being relegated from the 3. Liga each season, the sums don't add up.

An unsatisfactory solution is currently in place: the champions in the West and Southwest go up automatically while a third automatic promotion spot is rotated among the other three leagues in a three-year cycle. The fourth spot is allocated via a play-off between the winners of the remaining two leagues.

One champion always misses out and, increasingly, it's the champion from the Regional League Northeast, covering the territory of the former eastern German Democratic Republic (GDR).

In addition to Lok Leipzig's triple tragedy, former serial GDR Oberliga winners Dynamo Berlin fell short in 2022 and Energie Cottbus drew the short straw in 2023. This season, there is only one eastern German club in the 3. Liga: Hansa Rostock.

The struggles of the regions' football clubs are, to some degree, a result of continuing socio-economic disparities between east and west, which were also reflected in the success of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in recent state elections.

Even in 2026, not one of the 40 leading companies listed on Germany's DAX stock exchange is based in the former east (outside Berlin). Salaries remain lower, unemployment remains higher and the population is older and shrinking as young people move west.

The reason that automatic promotion spots are handed to the champions in the West and Southwest is simply because there are more men's football teams registered in those jurisdictions - because more people live there.

It is an argument that Ziane is tired of hearing.

"In that case, you might as well give us the automatic promotion spot because we attract bigger crowds," he says.

Indeed, the average attendance in the Regional League Northeast last season (3,125) was around twice as high as that in the other leagues. Lok Leipzig themselves had the fourth highest (6,352). More than 11,000 attended the local derby against city rivals Chemie Leipzig.

"Unfortunately, you don't get any points for tradition, crowds and history," says 39-year-old Lok chief executive Toni Wachsmuth, who does not have access to sponsors with the same financial firepower as his counterparts further west.

"The [western] leagues do have better economic foundations but everyone agrees that the current system is nonsense. Everyone needs to compromise but some officials are clearly putting their own interests and positions above the general good of German football."

It comes as little surprise, therefore, that the latest push for change has come from the east, with clubs launching a new campaign in March 2025 with the slogan: "Meister mussen aufsteigen!" â champions must go up!

Their proposal: a reduction from five leagues to four, with the precise geographical borders to be determined anew each season with the help of artificial intelligence, taking into account factors such as distance of travel to away games and attractive derbies.

They call it the compass model. Because it can go in all directions. In return, the Regional League Northeast is prepared to compromise by giving up its emotional attachment to the territory of the former East Germany.

"I want to get away from this east-west debate," says Tommy Haeder, the 35-year-old chief executive of Chemnitzer FC and figurehead of the reform campaign. "We've had a change of generation. Many older officials have retired and been replaced by younger people who don't have this nostalgia for the GDR."

Haeder also emphasises the benefits that a fairer promotion system would bring for German football as a whole, arguing that eastern clubs would be better equipped to continue nurturing youth talent.

"It's not in the interest of talent development when young footballers from Chemnitz are torn away from their homes and families at the age of 10 to join academies in Hamburg, Dortmund or Stuttgart," he tells BBC Sport.

"The compass model is a model in which every region sacrifices a little bit to solve a much bigger problem. We're organised, we have a plan, we've made suggestions. Now it's up to the federations to act."

The campaign has since gained the support of more than 80 clubs across Germany, from east to west and up and down the pyramid.

Union Berlin, who were playing in the fourth tier as recently as the 2000s, became the first Bundesliga club to officially back the initiative, with club president Dirk Zingler saying: "The current set-up contradicts our understanding of sporting competition."

Borussia Dortmund president â and Bundesliga chairman â Hans-Joachim Watzke added his influential voice, stating: "Champions must go up and we think the compass model with four regional leagues is the best option."

Support also has also come from Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose who, drawing on his past as both a player and coach at Lok Leipzig, said: "I know what it's like for clubs trying to work within their means, or lack of means, at that level. Everything is on a knife edge.

"You have to give the clubs and their fans the belief that their efforts and sacrifices will be rewarded with promotion."

Momentum was growing before a key vote at the end of June when, after months of discussions, clubs were finally set to vote on the compass model â but the ballot descended into farce when, at the last minute, the regional federations conducting the vote announced two key changes:

Suddenly, the four new leagues would consist of only 18 teams rather than 20 (thus making the compass model less attractive because 10 more teams would miss out), and a stipulation was added that a majority be reached in each of the five regions for the model to pass.

An overall majority (50.9%) in favour of the compass model was still reached (including 60.9% in the West, 61.5% in the North and 76.3% in the Northeast) but the Southwest voted for an alternative option in which the northeastern league would be dissolved and its clubs reallocated, while the Southwest and West would simply remain the same.

"The move from a functioning system to a complex, insecure and economically riskier model without an obvious benefit doesn't make any sense to me," Robert Lempka, chief executive of Regional League Southwest side FSV Frankfurt told local public broadcaster Hessischer Rundfunk this summer. "I find it unsettling that an untransparent algorithm should decide a club's future."

The Bavarians, meanwhile, voted vaguely for "further talks", with Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) President Christoph Kern telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper in August: "We've gathered our clubs together on several occasions and none of the suggested models have majority support. I'm not prepared to simply give up the Regional League Bavaria like that."

For Haeder in Chemnitz, the vote was "an absolute catastrophe â completely amateurish". And he's not alone.

This season, protests have erupted across German football. In the Regional League Northeast, almost every game has begun with a delay as players have simply refused to play for the first minute.

On the opening day, Lok Leipzig supporters, their team still stranded in the same division, threw hundreds of plastic trophies on to the pitch, symbolising the worthlessness of their club's back-to-back titles.

Down in Bavaria, Bayern Munich's ultras attended a reserve team game in the regional league and produced an intricate choreography criticising the Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) for what they perceive to be an unco-operative stance.

"You've taken us for fools long enough," read a banner beneath a display depicting BFV officials using a magnet to pull a compass needle towards them. The ultras then set off red pyrotechnics which turned the compass needle back in the direction of the fans.

And before the international break, fans of clubs across the Bundesliga used their platform to call for reform with co-ordinated banners reading: "Clubs and fans betrayed! Champions must go up! Compass model now!"

The compass, it would appear, may finally be pointing towards a resolution after the German Football Federation (DFB) announced the convening of an extraordinary general meeting on 18 December.

"[The issue] must be resolved," said President Bernd Neuendorf. "The compass model received the most votes and offers the best chance for a concentration of elite performance and therefore better development of talent."

Any changes would only be implemented in the 2028-29 season â too late for Ziane who, now 34, has embarked on his 13th season with Lok Leipzig. Back-to-back champions, but still in the fourth division.

"You can never completely get over it because, at our level, the 3. Liga is probably the pinnacle. Promotion with my hometown club would have been the most wonderful thing in the world for me," he says before heading out for training.

"It's a shame that we have to force ourselves to remember what we've achieved. It's so hard to win this league and we did it twice in a row! You can't take that for granted."

Mark Schwarzer had both struggles and important life experience during his two season playing in Germany as a youngster

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Even as the children of German emigrants, Mark Schwarzer found life in Germany in the mid-1990s difficult.

A 21-year-old Schwarzer moved halfway across the world to join Dynamo Dresden from the Sydney-based Marconi Stallions in 1994, but played just twice before making the move west to Kaiserslautern the following season.

That gave Schwarzer a glimpse of life in both sides of what was then still a newly-reunified country - and he admits it was an eye-opening experience for a young man.

Schwarzer told FourFourTwo: "I loved parts of it, I hated others.

"It was 1994, only four years after unification between East and West Germany. Dresden was a beautiful city but very run down, with a huge period of rebuilding going on.

"There was still a real divide between East and West, and it could be difficult to fit in.

"I was a foreigner – I was German, but I wasn’t, because I was born in Australia. I was kind of in no man’s land.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I spoke a little German, but the local dialect was really difficult to understand.

"Australians weren’t regarded that highly as footballers either. We had the odd good player, but we weren’t really respected.

"I only played two games that season, but in hindsight the experiences I gained were invaluable.

"Kaiserslautern was similar and there was still a lack of acceptance because of where I came from.

"I played four games, did well in two, but my last was definitely my worst performance.

"Then Otto Rehhagel came in. He wasn’t a fan of young players and didn’t rate me. After two-and-a-half years in Germany, I knew I needed to find a club where the manager wanted me.

"I’d always wanted to play in England, and my wife could work there more easily, so when Bradford came along in November 1996, it was a no-brainer."

#1040. Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono undecided on football return after Jesus de Miguel’s tragic death

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Jesus de Miguel died last week following an on-pitch collision with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

FC Andorra Carles Manso said on Thursday that goalkeeper Jesus Owono has not yet decided whether he will return to competition following the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.

De Miguel died in hospital on 4 November, the day after a collision with Owono on the pitch during a Spanish football match.

Owono, who is Equatorial Guinea's goalkeeper, released a statement through Andorra last week in which he described the ordeal as "the most difficult days of my life."

Manso has now offered an update on Jesus Owono, telling a press conference: "What we have to do is support him in every way and be close to him.

"We will give him space so that he feels completely free to make any decision, whether he wants to return, when, or if he does not want to return."

Manso said Owono was spending time with his family, friends and partner and described the aftermath of last week’s tragedy as a "very complicated situation to manage”.

"When he feels it is appropriate and when he feels genuinely ready to take a decision like that (he will do so)," added Manso.

Owono has 47 caps for Equatorial Guinea. He was not called up for his country's doubleheader with Zimbabwe during this international break.

Andorra travel to Almeria on Saturday for their first fixture since De Miguel's death.

Over the weekend, the Tenerife players and thousands of fans paid an emotional final tribute to De Miguel at the club’s stadium.

A massive banner displaying his black-and-white photograph and the words "Forever Demi", a reference to the player’s nickname, hung behind a central pitch stage at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez.

Following a video showing footage of his Tenerife debut, fans chanted: "De Miguel, we love you".

Players sat beside representatives from all clubs in Spain's top two divisions, including Real Madrid director Emilio Butragueno, as tears fell in the stands.

"To speak of you in the past tense is tremendously unfair," Tenerife captain Enric Gallego said, pausing repeatedly during his speech.

"It's still hard to believe that this has happened to us, Demi; you'll always be one of us."

"We're still struggling to come to terms with the fact that you won't be with us again.”

#1039. Scotland without captain Weir for World Cup play-off

Weir has scored 32 goals in 122 Scotland appearances

Scotland will be without captain Caroline Weir for the World Cup play-off final with Sweden following a setback in her recovery from a muscle injury.

The influential midfielder pulled up in the warm-up before the win over Czech Republic in Paisley a month ago and has not played for Lyon since.

Aston Villa forward Mia McAulay is also missing after a recent calf problem, with Beth Lumsden of Newcastle and Ipswich striker Eilidh Adams added to the squad.

"Of course we're disappointed for Caroline," said head coach Melissa Andreatta. "She's our captain and she has spoken about how much she loves this team.

"But for us, it's all about the players that we have. Our focus is on working together and doing whatever it takes to be on the right side of the result."

Sweden visit Paisley for the first leg on 1 December, with the return game in Stockholm on 5 December.

Andreatta on Weir missing out on play-off final

BBC Scotland will broadcast the opening game while the action in Sweden will be shown by BBC ALBA.

Victory could secure Scotland's spot at Brazil 2027, although there remains the possibility of an intercontinental play-off in February for Europe's lowest ranked play-off final winner.

Sweden have been at every World Cup since the inaugural tournament in 1991 and finished third at the last two editions.

"We don't fear anybody," added Andreatta.

"We have a squad full of quality and we have shown our character and what we are all about.

"I'm confident and that comes from our preparation and our experience."

#1038. Kane bends game to his will on record-breaking night

One day it will have to end for Harry Kane, but for now, almost 12 years into his England life, there is still no matching the wisdom and influence he has accumulated over all those games and all those goals for his country.

This would have been a great night by any measure for a man collecting his record-breaking 126th England cap. There was a handshake from Peter Shilton, now deposed as king of caps, and a flourish by Kane of his recently acquired Ballon d’Or, once his four children had accompanied him on to the pitch. These are the nights of which dreams are made, and yet – given the defining feature of Kane’s career – there was one more thing to accomplish.

That was a goal from the man who has ploughed relentlessly past the two great England individual landmarks of caps and goals. His second-half penalty won the game and, although he is not infallible from the spot, he is as close to that status as England have ever had. Age has not yet run him down, he can still bend the game to his will, and when it comes to the pressure moments, his longevity seems to offer the upper hand.

This was always going to be Kane’s night, with a great banner on the west side of the stadium paying tribute to the England captain. The Prince of Wales was in attendance for the occasion, too. Luka Modric presented his former Tottenham Hotspur team-mate with a keepsake from the Croatian football federation. Kane had to wait for the second half for the most valuable offering of all.

After the hour, the Danish referee Morten Krogh was advised by his VAR Bastian Dankert to take a second look at a corner tangle involving Jarell Quansah, and decided to award the second-half penalty from which Kane scored. It was certainly clumsy, but these grapples have been overlooked by referees in the past. The 27th successfully converted penalty of the Kane England era followed, and the man himself played the full game.

Afterwards, Kane made a point of thanking the Football Association for organising it all, although it was also clear that this was no less than he expected. “It’s important to recognise the great players,” he said, “and it’s not something we have always done over the years.”

If the sentiment was a little awkwardly articulated, he is certainly right on the key point: so many England careers have ended abruptly at tournament elimination or elsewhere. Yet here was one being celebrated with the man himself, in what might even be argued to be his prime. Kane, 33, was asked again as to how long he might continue and did not rule out going on to 40, “if I’m performing at the highest level”.

That was a nod to Modric, a second-half substitute at the age of 41 and now on 207 caps for Croatia and almost 1,200 senior games. This Croatia team still seem unable to part company with their greatest player, despite his struggles against England in the seven-goal defeat in Rijeka. On this occasion, Croatia were much better.

It should have been more straightforward for England. They had taken the lead through Morgan Rogers midway through the first half and had dominated the first hour. But Quansah’s mistake gave Croatia an equaliser, and after Kane’s penalty England were fortunate to survive on occasions.

“It was a tight match – a tough one,” Thomas Tuchel, the England manager, said. “We didn’t take our chances when we had chances, so it stayed a tight match. It cannot be glamorous and super-exciting [all the time]. It has to be serious and determined. We wanted a final on Sunday in Spain and we have that.”

The win means that England’s game in Madrid on Sunday against Spain, who beat the Czech Republic and lead the Nations League group by three points, has some bite to it. Another England win would mean they would overtake Spain on goal difference and win the group ahead of the Nations League quarter-finals in March.

This was one game when the players might have wondered if they were due more from a Wembley crowd that went through the motions in the first half and scarcely returned for the second. For the first hour, England dominated a Croatia side who often invited six blue shirts into their back line. Tuchel said his decision to select Dan Burn in the left-sided centre-half position over the left-footed Jarrad Branthwaite was almost split – a “51 per cent decision”.

England would break through just once, when Rogers got enough of his laces on an awkward Jude Bellingham cross deflected behind him and the shot brushed Josko Gvardiol on the way in.

Trent Alexander-Arnold started his third England game of the autumn and the right-back spent most of it in midfield. From the left it was his pass to Bellingham on the right wing that prefaced the cross for the Rogers goal.

The catastrophe of the defeat last month for Croatia meant they were naturally conservative. Nevertheless, in Martin Baturina, the 23-year-old Como attacking midfielder, they have another fine talent. When Modric did come on, he was applauded on all sides of Wembley. The equaliser was a Quansah error when the defender tried to head a loose corner back to Jordan Pickford and did not make the distance. Petar Sucic intervened and pushed it home with a right foot. Kane scored that and the substitute James Garner had a goal disallowed in the closing stages of the game, which were much less comfortable for England.

“Got a little bit sloppy at the very end of the first half, started the second half very good, didn’t score the second goal, conceded from a set piece, and then showed a good reaction.

On whether England were sloppy when they conceded: “It was maybe only three or four minutes before we gave passes away and especially in a moment when we were clearly the better team, we came with a very strong reaction after the half-time, had a beautiful chance created from Declan Rice and they blocked it on the line. Harry Kane has now scored 92 goals in 126 appearances for England.

Thomas Tuchel has said he has “unfinished business” with England and will remain in his position for the Euros in 2028, but did say that he would return to club football after seeing out his contract.

“I signed the contract, I want to stay until the Euros,” he said this week. “I want to do the Euros. We have unfinished business.”

But he added: “I miss the 50 matches [a season].

“I miss the two minutes when everything is done. You go out two minutes before the whistle goes, it’s like the best two minutes, everything is done and you’re in a full stadium, lights are on and you’re just so excited and you’re part of it.”

Shortly before kick-off, Croatia captain Luka Modric will present England captain Harry Kane with a special gift from the Croatian Football Federation (HNS), marking his Ballon d’Or win and his achievement in becoming England’s all-time record appearance holder with 126 caps.

Modric is not in the starting line-up but the 41-year-old has 206 caps for his country and will present Kane with a specially crafted replica of the first football ever brought to Croatia, which English industrialists introduced to the town of Zupanja in 1880. This event is regarded as the beginning of organised football on Croatian soil.

England’s 3-0 home victory over Czech Republic last month left them on nine points after four Nations League group games.

It came after a 2-0 win in the away contest, a 7-0 thumping of Croatia and a 3-2 defeat against world champions Spain.

A draw tonight will be enough for Thomas Tuchel’s side to book their place in the quarter-finals of the competition.

The eight teams to finish in the top two of the four League A groups will play in the knockout rounds that start in March 2027.

The two worst sides to finish bottom are automatically relegated, while the other bottom sides and third-placed sides are at risk of relegation via a play-off.

Few expect Jobe to be better than his older brother. While Jobe will make his England debut just two months after turning 21, Jude’s first cap came aged 17. By the time that he was Jobe’s age now, Jude had already thrived for England in two international tournaments. But Jobe has one major sporting advantage: he is the younger sibling.

Younger siblings have significantly more chance of becoming elite athletes. If two siblings both become professional, the little sibling is significantly more likely to enjoy the better career.

Jude and Jobe Bellingham could become the first brothers to start for England since Gary and Phil Neville took to the field together 19 years ago, with Jobe included in his first senior squad.

Jack and Bobby Charlton are the only other brothers to play together for England in the post-war period.

“I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said on the FA’s England app as he discussed his call-up.

“It’s quite special, to be honest. It’s such a huge bonus on top of something that’s already so special and so great. To be called up for England is a dream itself and I’ve been so proud to have the opportunity to represent England at every age group.

“I always enjoyed coming away with England, I love competing against top players at whichever age group. But to have that chance of an opportunity to represent England with my brother, it’s really hard to put into words.

“I don’t have the words, really. I think it’s only emotion that could describe it, and, hopefully, if that time does come, you’ll see a lot of emotion from people, and definitely from my family.”

There will be a special pre-match presentation to honour Harry Kane becoming England’s record appearance maker, with 126 caps, overtaking Peter Shilton. Shilton has held the record since 1989.

The goalkeeper is at Wembley to formally mark Kane’s achievement. The England captain will also show the Ballon d’Or trophy he won last month.

Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph from last month will also be celebrated tonight before kick-off, along with his record appearance.

“I think I maybe underappreciated how big it was going to be, how big the reaction was going to be,” he told the BBC.

“It’s just been crazy, whether it’s messages on my phone or on social media, or people calling me, and just being in the street and everyone congratulating me.

“I think the actual moment when Ronaldo said my name, it’s strange, it’s almost like a movie.

“In the moment, it was like in slow motion and the confetti was supposed to fall and all this, but when I watched it back, I had my hand to my mouth and maybe a couple of seconds and I was out, but in the actual moment, it felt like I was doing it for a minute.

“It was a really unique feeling because it is different to playing a game or scoring a goal, because it is so individual, it is nothing you can kind of do.

“Your mind is playing games with you the whole night, whether it is going to be you or not.

“So, when he actually said my name, it was just a crazy emotion.”

To the exclusive club of Billy Wright, Sir Bobby Charlton, Bobby Moore and Peter Shilton, the name Harry Kane will be added on Thursday night. It is only the fifth time that a new men’s England international appearance record has been set in the post-war era, with Kane preparing for his 126th England match to surpass a landmark that has stood for 36 years.

“I’ll be the first to congratulate him because I think he’s done it the right way,” says Shilton, who will be back at Wembley to metaphorically pass on the baton.

“He’s not coming on as a substitute; he’s been out there every game, doing his job. Records are there to be beaten and I couldn’t think of anybody better than Harry, not just on the pitch but off the pitch. I am very proud of the record and handing it to Harry makes it not quite as bad.

“I think striker is the hardest position to play and goalkeeper is the second hardest because of the responsibility you’ve got. But scoring goals is the most difficult thing and Harry’s record in the modern game is there to be seen.”

Thomas Tuchel has said Harry Kane was the deserved winner of the Ballon d’Or, with the England head coach describing the striker as “an extraordinary player”.

“He wins the Ballon d’Or, and deservedly so, and in the next game for England he gets the all-time record with 126 matches,” Tuchel said when announcing the latest squad.

“Thursday is a deserved occasion to celebrate an extraordinary player.”

Kane said: “It’s not about me – it’s about the team. I love coming to every England camp. I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible.”

Harry Kane starts for England in what will be a record 126th appearance for his country.

Thomas Tuchel makes three changes from last month’s win over Czech Republic, with Dan Burn, Declan Rice and Anthony Gordon replacing Marc Guehi, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Eberechi Eze.

Harry Kane will become England’s record appearance maker this evening, with the 33-year-old set to earn his 126th cap.

The striker started his international career against Lithuania in March 2015, scoring just 79 second after replacing Wayne Rooney at Wembley.

Eight years later, Kane surpassed Rooney as the country’s record goalscorer, netting his 54th England goal in an away contest with Italy.

He equalled Peter Shilton’s record of 125 caps last month against Czech Republic as he scored his 90th and 91st international goals.

England will be hoping for a repeat of their fixture against Croatia last month, with Thomas Tuchel’s side producing an emphatic 7-0 victory in Rijeka.

England were 4-0 up at half-time of the Nations League contest, which was attended by 6,000 schoolchildren and 100 visiting fans, with Croatia supporters sanctioned over previous bad behaviour.

England’s front four of Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka were all on the scoresheet in the opening period, with Kane and Saka doubling their tallies in the second half before a late seventh from Morgan Rogers.

Good evening and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of England vs Croatia in the Nations League, with the hosts’ captain Harry Kane set to become the country’s most-capped player.

The 33-year-old has enjoyed a memorable few weeks, becoming the first English Ballon d’Or winner in 25 years and following it up with a new Bayern Munich contract, and an appearance at Wembley tonight will take him clear of Peter Shilton’s record of 125 England caps.

Kane scored twice in his record-equalling appearance against Czech Republic at Wembley last month, extending his international tally to 91 goals – a total that is unrivalled for England.

“It’s not about me – it’s about the team,” Kane said before tonight’s landmark moment. “I love coming to every England camp. I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible.”

The 3-0 home victory over Czech Republic left England on nine points after four Nations League group games, with a 2-0 win in the away contest and a 7-0 thumping of Croatia coming after a 3-2 defeat against world champions Spain.

Thomas Tuchel will be hoping that his side can inflict another heavy defeat on Croatia this evening, but a draw will be enough to book their place in the quarter-finals, with the group’s top two teams progressing.

While Kane will collect plaudits for his 126th cap, attention will also be on a potential first, with Jude Bellingham’s younger brother, Jobe, included in a senior England squad for the first time.

The two Bellinghams appearing together in a senior match would be a new experience for them, while it would be the first time that brothers have taken to the field together for England in 19 years.

“I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said on the Football Association’s England app. “It’s quite special, to be honest. It’s such a huge bonus on top of something that’s already so special and so great.”

Since Mauricio Pochettino arrived in English football with Southampton in January 2013, Manchester United have cycled through a dozen interim, caretaker or permanent managers, from Sir Alex Ferguson to Michael Carrick.

Even more coaches have been linked with the post, with the same names seemingly popping up every time the Old Trafford dugout is vacant.

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Mauricio Pochettino is one such manager and, according to the man himself, this was not just gossip column speculation.

The Argentine was first linked with Manchester United a decade ago, speculation that gathered pace when he met Sir Alex Ferguson for lunch in 2016, during which time he was in charge of Spurs.

“United have always shown interest,” Pochettino revealed to FourFourTwo in an interview earlier this year. “But the ideal scenario to manage there has never quite materialised.

“In any case, that lunch with Sir Alex had absolutely nothing to do with it,” he continues before explaining how the meeting came about.

“In his final season as a manager, we played a great game against United with Southampton. In the press conference after, he said we’d been the most complete opponent that United had faced.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“Through the secretary of the League Managers Association, he asked for my phone number so that we could have lunch. It was a meeting in London between colleagues – between a genius and an apprentice.

“My English wasn’t great, but Jesus Perez helped. When we asked for the bill, I wanted to take it, and so did he. We started arguing over who’d pay! “He said, “Stop Mauricio, I’m going to ask you a question. If you answer correctly, you pay. If not, I’ll pay.” I had no idea what he was going to ask.

“He said, “Name an Argentine player who scored in the 1930 World Cup final.” I replied, “Stabile.” He couldn’t believe it. The name came to me out of nowhere! In the end, I paid the bill.”

Speculation mounted again six years later in 2022, when the Red Devils would eventually go on to appoint Erik ten Hag.

“I was under contract at PSG,” Pochettino continues. “After our Champions League elimination against Real Madrid, we had no option but to make sure we secured the Ligue 1 title at least.

“United were in a hurry to announce their new manager before the end of that season because the situation had become unsustainable. I couldn’t negotiate, whereas Ajax gave Ten Hag the flexibility to do so.”

Pochettino is widely expected to replace Carrick in the dugout at Old Trafford ahead of Man United's derby with Liverpool later this month.

The Argentine coach is reported to have a $10 million break clause in his USMNT contract, which was extended over the summer following the United States' World Cup campaign.

Man United chiefs are meeting in Monaco this week to discuss the club's next steps.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

#1036. Goodwillie prosecutors 'wrong' not to put footballer on trial for rape, court hears

David Goodwillie was ruled to be a rapist at a civil court hearing in 2017

The lawyer for a woman raped by former Scotland international footballer David Goodwillie said prosecutors made a "mistake" in not putting him on trial for the attack.

A civil action found Denise Clair was raped by Goodwillie and his then-Dundee United teammate David Robertson at a flat in Armadale, West Lothian in January 2011.

Her lawyer, Thomas Ross KC, has argued the Crown Office "got it wrong" in deciding to drop rape charges against him due to "insufficient evidence".

Clair has brought an action to the Court of Criminal Appeal in Edinburgh to grant permission for a rare private prosecution against Goodwillie.

Ross told judges Lord Pentland, Lord Matthews and Lady Carmichael that it was "inevitable" errors in pursuing prosecutions would be made.

On the first day of the hearing, Ross said the prosecution service received between "150,000 to 200,000" reports to consider each year.

Legal aid approved for private rape prosecution

Goodwillie victim 'in limbo' over criminal trial

He said a "substantial body of evidence" had been provided in Clair's case before judges threw out the claim in July 2011.

Ross described the decision not to prosecute as "irrational", adding: "There was a sufficient body of evidence available which would have allowed a prosecution to proceed and there was a reasonable chance of conviction.

"Our position is that in the circumstances the Crown have got it wrong."

Alan Cameron KC, for the Crown, told the court that prosecutors had acted correctly when it decided not to prosecute Goodwillie.

He said that when all the evidence available in the case was considered, the Crown were entitled not to bring Goodwillie to court.

Cameron added: "There are no exceptional circumstances which would permit the issuing of criminal letters."

Clair previously chose to identify herself in the case.

She claimed she had been on a night out in Bathgate on 1 January before returning to a flat with Goodwillie and Robertson in the early hours of the following morning.

She alleged the footballers took advantage of her when she was vulnerable due to being intoxicated and raped her.

Both men had denied the charges, but Clair brought a civil action against them in January 2017.

The judge who heard that case at the Court of Session, Lord Armstrong, ruled both of the men to be rapists and ordered them to pay Clair Â£100,000 in damages.

It was the first civil rape case of its kind in Scotland.

Denise Clair, pictured during the civil court case in 2017

However, Clair is now seeking a private criminal prosecution.

The court heard that, for the action to be successful, Clair's lawyers must prove that prosecutors had made a decision that "no reasonable" prosecutors could have made.

The legal test was described as being of a "high standard".

The court heard evidence given by Goodwillie during the civil case could be used in any private prosecution.

His lawyer, Lord Stewart of Dirleton KC, said the legal tests needed to bring a private prosecution were not passed.

Lord Stewart also argued the use of evidence given by Goodwillie during the civil case in this new case was unfair.

He said: "The evidence proceeded on the Lord Advocate having renounced the right to prosecute.

"Had it been clear that a prosecution was going to follow, then the Lord Advocate should have issued a warning."

David Goodwillie made three appearances for Scotland

Goodwillie earned three caps for the Scottish national team, scoring once in a match against World Cup holders Spain in October 2011.

At the time of the incident, he was playing for Dundee United, but went on to represent Aberdeen, Ross County and Clyde in the Scottish professional game.

He also played for the English clubs Blackburn Rovers, Crystal Palace and Plymouth Argyle.

Goodwillie joined Scottish Championship club Raith Rovers from Clyde in January 2022, but the transfer caused a number of club officials, women's team players and volunteers to resign.

Author Val McDermid also withdrew her sponsorship of the club's shirts.

Goodwillie returned to Clyde, but further controversy forced the loan deal to be cancelled and he was released by Raith Rovers in September 2022.

He has since played for a number of amateur and semi-professional clubs, lastly Glasgow United, whom he left in the summer.

Lord Pentland, Scotland's most senior judge, said the appeal court would take time to consider all submissions.

He said a judgement would be issued "as soon as practicable".

Mauricio Pochettino is expected to be named as the new Manchester United manager

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mauricio Pochettino has never shied away from the scale of the jobs he undertakes, which perhaps explains why he's willing to take the reins at Manchester United.

With Michael Carrick’s tenure set to end following a return of just one win from ten Premier League matches, the Argentine is in the frame to replace him in the Old Trafford dugout, setting up a head-to-head with former employers Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea.

Reflecting on his summer 2023 arrival in west London, Pochettino offered FourFourTwo an uncompromising assessment of the environment he inherited under co-owner Todd Boehly and Clearlake Capital.

"Chelsea were broken when I arrived," Pochettino revealed. "There were young players making their debuts that season, and there had been many defeats at Stamford Bridge. The momentum was negative. The aim was to stop the slide, start building again, restore belief and give the players the chance to perform.

Despite the friction of a bloated dressing room, Pochettino engineered a late turnaround, ultimately steering Chelsea back into Europe.

"We ended that season by winning five straight league games and finished in sixth – if we’d had one more month, we would have qualified for the Champions League," he added.

On-pitch progress aside, Pochettino's departure was confirmed days after the season concluded. He insists the decision to walk was entirely driven from his side of the table.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I didn’t want to continue. That was my decision. I spoke with Chelsea, but my staff and I were clear about our position. We felt we didn’t belong to the club’s way of doing things. We helped stabilise Chelsea, but had no interest in staying."

The reflections arrive at a critical time for Manchester United with chief executive Omar Berrada and technical director Jason Wilcox holding summit talks with Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco to discuss the club's future.

Pochettino has emerged as the clear frontrunner to stop the rot during the November international break.

Prising him away from the United States Men’s National Team (USMNT) carries a steep price tag, with his release clause understood to sit around $10m.

But, Pochettino's proven track record of restoring order to dysfunctional dressing rooms makes him a top candidate for Old Trafford.

His Chelsea post-mortem also sends an implicit message to Man United minority owners INEOS: he is capable of halting a freefall, but will not tolerate working under an ownership model at odds with his sporting philosophy.

#1034. Gary Neville explains why Mauricio Pochettino is the right manager for Man United

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Pochettino looks set to replace Michael Carrick in the Old Trafford dugout and Neville hopes he can succeed

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Gary Neville has spoken out on the reports that Mauricio Pochettino will become the new manager of Manchester United following the sacking of Michael Carrick on Thursday.

Carrick was let go with United sitting 18th in the Premier League table and having won just one league match of the 2026/27 season.

United States manager Pochettino has reportedly reached a verbal agreement with the club to replace Carrick and an announcement of his appointment is expected soon.

The Old Trafford hierarchy will need to pay compensation to secure Pochettino’s services but they expect to get a deal done for the Argentine to take charge before United’s next fixture on November 22.

Former United captain Neville appeared on Sky Sports News after news broke of Carrick’s firing and explained why Pochettino could be the right man for the club.

“I’ve always, and I think this is public knowledge... I’ve always wanted Mauricio Pochettino as manager at [Manchester] United,” said Neville.

“I’ve said that numerous times, back when Jose Mourinho was maybe coming to Manchester United, I think maybe when Erik ten Hag came to Manchester United.

“I think he’s a brilliant person, I think he’ll handle the media, I think he understands the size of the club but it’s a monumental task to win everybody else over and get everybody on side and make sure he has a team that can compete.

“But he’s a brilliant coach with great experience and he’s a good man. And I think he also believes in young players and bringing players through and developing them and coaching them, which is what he’s going to have to do at Manchester United.

“I’ve always liked Mauricio Pochettino, whether this is the right point for him to take the Manchester United job, who knows?

“We’ll find out in the next year or two but I’m hoping that he’s made some pretty strong demands on the way in and he’s got control of the club.”

#1031. Largs get floodlights consent in time for cup tie with Ayr – watch on BBC

Largs Thistle lost to Auchinleck Talbot in last season's Scottish Junior Cup final

The Scottish Cup third-round tie between Largs Thistle and Ayr United will be shown live on the BBC Scotland channel, website and iPlayer on Friday, 27 November, with a 19:30 kick-off.

It comes after the Lowland League West club gained permission from North Ayrshire Council to keep the floodlights on at their Barrfields Park until 22:00 GMT.

They previously were only permitted to operate the pitch and floodlights at the 4,500-capacity stadium beyond a 21:00 cut-off on no more than two nights in any calendar month.

Following Largs' promotion from the West of Scotland League Premier Division to Scotland's fifth tier, which requires 19:45 midweek kick-offs, the previous restriction had already resulted in the club moving midweek matches 11 miles away to Ardrossan.

Watch: Morton stun Stenny, Cove humble Accies & Clyde keep pace

Ayr travel the 33 miles north to meet Ayrshire rivals who are making their debut in the competition having reached their highest-ever placing in senior football.

Former Queen of the South midfielder Stuart Davidson's Largs lost to Auchinleck Talbot in the final of last season's Scottish Junior Cup and currently sit second in the Lowland League, one point behind Ayrshire rivals Kilwinning Rangers.

They have reached the Scottish Cup third round after away victories over two Lowland League East sides - 1-0 against Gala Fairydean Rovers and a 5-1 thrashing of Dunipace.

Gary Naysmith's Ayr, who enter the Scottish Cup at the third-round stage, are currently seventh in the second-tier Championship and reached the fourth round last season before losing to Dundee United.

Liverpool have gazumped Chelsea for their first signing of the winter window, as Andoni Iraola's side takes shape

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool have a deal in place for their first signing of the January transfer window.

The Reds enjoyed a solid summer improving their options in attack and defence, with nine-figure Bradley Barcola leading the charge, and Jeremy Jacquet, Ronald Araujo and Victor Munoz also signing.

But with Liverpool still somewhat lacking in the centre of the park, manager Andoni Iraola's next buy will address fans' concerns about the lack of bite in midfield.

After Chelsea's electric start suggested new manager Xabi Alonso could muster a title challenge, the Blues have encountered a few stumbling blocks, with slow-starting Liverpool now above them in the table.

Iraola and Alonso both know each other from growing up in the Basque Country, and the former may now pip the latter to a signing that could transform either club's season.

According to Anfield Index, journalist Lewis Steele of the Daily Mail claimed that Lamine Camara is a name that “won't go away”.

“Chelsea sources I’ve spoken to believe Liverpool may have a deal in place with the player,” Steele mentioned, adding, “Trey Nyoni being brilliant but only 19, you do wonder if this is one [sporting director Julian] Ward could bring forward.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Last month, TEAMtalk revealed that Liverpool had stepped up efforts to land the Monaco midfielder when they were knocked back in a move for controversial Borussia Dortmund man, Felix Nmecha.

Chelsea had a deal in place for Camara towards the end of the transfer window, but the move was called off when Monaco pulled the plug.

The principality outfit were in the process of selling Folarin Balogun to Everton, too, when the United States international pulled out of his medical and refused to travel to Merseyside – with both players remaining in Ligue 1.

Liverpool began the campaign with Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch in a double-pivot, though they lacked defensive awareness, with better form coming since the teenage Nyoni was drafted into the centre.

FourFourTwo understands that the Reds are on the hunt for full-backs and another right-winger, too, in the upcoming window.

Camara is worth €55 million, according to Transfermarkt. Liverpool face Manchester United when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

Pep Guardiola is a “top target” to become the next USA head coach with Mauricio Pochettino set to leave the role and become Manchester United manager.

Michael Carrick was finally sacked by United on Thursday morning and, as The Independent first reported a few days ago, Pochettino is being lined up for a return to club football to take over at Old Trafford.

The deal is currently being finalised, with an official announcement expected relatively soon, although the specifics of when exactly the Argentine will leave his USMNT role is not yet clear, with a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final clash against Haiti taking place on Saturday and Tuesday.

Whether Pochettino remains in charge for those two matches or not, the US will soon have to embark on a search for a new coach and The Athletic are reporting that ex-Manchester City boss Guardiola is their preferred early choice.

Guardiola left Man City after 10 trophy-laden years – the legitimacy of some of which have been thrown into doubt with the club being found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial rules – this summer and is yet to return to management. US Soccer has reportedly discussed the Spaniard internally as a candidate across multiple levels of the federation’s hiring process.

It certainly would not be an easy appointment, with the 55-year-old being the leading, currently available coach in world football and showing no rush to jump back into management after the end of his City tenure.

He was in the frame for the Italy job a couple of months ago but turned them down, with Italian football federation president Giovanni Malago telling La Repubblica: “Pep was honest. He took a sabbatical, partly for family reasons, but if he’d done anything, he would have done it with us.” Instead, Roberto Mancini returned to manage the Azzurri for a second time.

Guardiola is reported to have long been intrigued by the prospect of working in the United States, and enjoyed his time in New York during a year-long sabbatical after leaving Barcelona in 2012 – including the relative anonymity of living in the US’ biggest City.

He has previously had discussions with US Soccer, who have long been keen to attract him to the role and when Pochettino was appointed in 2024, Guardiola wished him luck.

He said in a press conference: “The USA is fascinating to try to build a project for many years and being able to get the national team to the next step. The potential with the USA is there for the amount of people and sports and so on.”

After the two-legged quarter-final with Haiti, the US won’t have another competitive game until March (although will have a training camp, mainly for domestic players, in December outside an official international window) giving them plenty of time to conduct a thorough managerial search and potentially allowing Guardiola a few more months away from football before diving back into management.

#1027. Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row

The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes

They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year.

Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running, but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.

As the Top 100 approaches a decade since its inception, nobody has quite dominated an era like Bonmatí and, while 2025 did not end in major silverware on the European stage, there were moments of sublime brilliance on the way to a Champions League final as well as the Euro one with Spain.

Bonmatí, as the very best do, has become a figure who can step up when needed most, and has become synonymous with the Blaugrana Barcelona stripes, a one-club woman with over 300 appearances in all competitions for the Catalan giants. Catalonia born and bred, both her parents were teachers of the Catalan language, with Bonmatí’s life and career intertwined with the region since she was a child, and now she has become an icon not just at home, but all around the world.

In a time where the women’s game is growing exponentially and world class talents are queueing up to dethrone the midfielder, she remains at the top. However, having broken a leg in training before the Nations League final she will miss more than four months of 2026. She will be sorely missed.

It was a tighter margin of victory in 2025, 453 points ahead of compatriot Mariona Caldentey – compared to 568 last year ahead of Caroline Graham Hansen – with the Spanish duo plus Alessia Russo and Putellas all gaining over 4,000 points from our record panel of 143 judges.

Bonmatí received 43% of the No 1 votes, ahead of Caldentey with a 21% share. Russo and Putellas both had 8% of the first picks in third and fourth respectively.

In a year where England backed up their Euro 2022 success with victory in Switzerland, Brazil continued their dominance in South America and Nigeria regained supremacy in Africa, it was all change across the top 100 as players such as Caldentey, Russo, Hannah Hampton, Temwa Chawinga, Patri Guijarro, Ewa Pajor and Clàudia Pina all made a new-look top 10 for the first time.

The Barcelona starlet Pina was the biggest mover, up 65 places on 2024, followed by another Spaniard in Gotham FC striker Esther González, up 59, while Klara Bühl moved up 40, just ahead of Russo’s 39 to propel the Arsenal striker into the top three.

Ghizlane Chebbak gave Morocco a first ever entry into the top 100 and Canada’s new Northern Super League was represented in its first year thanks to the Nigerian striker Esther Okoronkwo of AFC Toronto.

In fact, almost a quarter of this year’s 100 were brand new faces, emphasising just how fast the women’s game is growing, with the Chelsea and England shot-stopper Hampton the highest of the new names, shooting straight into the top five after her Euro-winning performances, while Vicky López, Sofia Cantore, Nathalie Björn and Michelle Agyemang all made the top 50.

Performances on the continental stage earned first-time appearances for the likes of Okoronkwo, Brazil’s Amanda Gutierres and Nigeria’s Gift Monday, while potential stars of the future such as Olivia Smith, Lily Yohannes and Signe Gaupset ranked for the first time. Mexico’s Charlyn Corral gained long overdue recognition.

Others made their way back into the 100, such as the Arsenal and England duo Leah Williamson and Chloe Kelly after a trophy-laden 12 months while Sandy Baltimore and Cristiana Girelli also made returns straight into the top quarter.

Lucy Bronze, Wendie Renard and Pernille Harder remain the only three players to have maintained a place every year after Saki Kumagai and Jenni Hermoso dropped out for the first time and it was Bronze’s Chelsea who dethroned Barcelona as the team with the most representatives with 15 compared to Arsenal’s 14 and Barcelona’s 12 after a domestic treble for Sonia Bompastor’s side.

Unsurprisingly after another Euro success, England pip Spain as the nation with the most players, 14 to 13, followed by the USA and France with nine each, while Copa América winners Brazil move into the top five for the first time with five players of their own.

The Women’s Super League asserts its dominance with 39 players on the list, up 12 from 2024, ahead of the NWSL with 19 and Liga F with 16. Players such as Jess Park, Aoba Fujino, Mary Fowler and Maya Le Tissier just missed out.

The young and old were once again represented at either end of the spectrum, with Marta again the oldest representative, the 39-year-old playing a key role in Brazil’s Copa América success with a dramatic late goal in the final against Colombia to keep their hopes alive. The OL Lyonnes and USA superstar Yohannes is the youngest at 18 and one of three teenagers to rank alongside López and Agyemang.

But it is again Bonmatí who ranks above them all, asserting her authority as one of the greatest of the modern era.

#1026. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

If someone would've said to me I'd be doing this as a job when I was 12, I wouldn't have believed them.

My name's Jacob. I'm a content creator, and I work with Bolton Wanderers.

My role here at Bolton is coming up with new ideas for social media, to try new concepts, filming stuff, and then posting them onto Bolton's pages and trying to help people follow the club. In my opinion, I think it's one of the funnest jobs in football, and it's brilliant.

Right. Welcome to Bolton, Larra. I hope I said that right. I'm going to teach you some Bolton twang to help you settle in.

My passion for football when I was growing up started at a very young age. My dad used to take me to the football matches, and I got my very first season ticket when I was five years old in the 2010/11 season, when Bolton was in the Premiership. Being something I loved as a kid, to turn it into my job is amazing.

I work here at least two days a week, obviously filming content, producing content,and then on match day, I'll be filming mostly with fans, and I love it.

As a town? Well, for us, it's lovely. Yeah.

Mondays, meetings. We have the marketing meeting, so that gives you an idea of what the week holds, what I'm going to do on a match day with the fans. And then in the week, I either film in with players, retail, commercial,whatever department needs help producing videos.

Some of the skills I use, I think one of them's got to be communication. You've got to be able to talk to people, talk to fans, and if you're watching this and you're a bit shy, or you think you can't communicate with people as well, I was like that inhigh school, so you learn it as you get older. But working in football, you've got to be adaptable because one minute you're doing a new signing, next minute you're working with the players, next minute it's a match day, next minute the season's over.

I'd say another one is being creative. That's probably the most important one because without being creative, you won't be able to put a video together.

So when I was 16 in high school, that's where my journey started. I did videos, which got me a number of followers. I always struggled in the classroom side in high school, but creating content and creating ideas and being creative, I was always really, really good at in high school, whether that would be doing something drama-related or English, writing, creating stories. I always knew I had a passion for creative pieces of work and being able to now do it as a job, it suits me down to the ground.

I didn't go to college. I didn't go to uni. I left high school with no GCSEs, but I've always had a real passion for football, so that's how I got in contact with Bolton Wanderers. I started doing some videos here at Bolton with the fans and that, and then it turned into going to the training ground and filming with the players, working with the commercial team, retail team, all the different departmentsaround the football club to eventually getting a paid role in football.

I think don't wait for an opportunity to come to you. Get out there and try. If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role there. But if it doesn't, then you've also created a portfolio working with different people, different businesses, different companies, and it's really good for your CV and for future opportunities with different companies.

The highlight of my career so far, probably looking back, being resilient enough to create my own career path in doing something I love.

When you score this season, you might be chuffed.

If you're passionate about football, you're a bit creative, and you're good in front of the camera, content creation infootball might be a job for you.

To find out what other careers you can have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, coming up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posting them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

England have called up Jobe Bellingham - and the data says it makes perfect sense

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Jobe Bellingham's England call-up isn't the first to come under scrutiny, and it certainly won't be the last.

But it is somewhat cruel that the midfielder's first-ever international appearance looks to be met with weary suspicion that it's down to connections rather than what he can actually do on the pitch.

Because the truth is, England could actually do with Jobe Bellingham – despite the embarrassment of riches that the Three Lions have in that area of the pitch.

Thomas Tuchel has Jude Bellingham as his first-choice No.10. Beyond that, Morgan Rogers, Morgan Gibbs-White, Eberechi Eze, Cole Palmer and Phil Foden have all competed for that position over the past 18 months.

Each of them offers something a little different to Bellingham: Eze and Palmer, for example, have the deftness of pass, while Foden and Rogers are capable of arriving at the edge of the box for a finesse finish into the bottom corner.

But Jobe is a stylistic replacement for Jude, and the data backs it up: looking at stats courtesy of Gradient Sports, Bellingham the younger ranks third out of our seven candidates for open play shooting – which measures a player's individual execution and decision-making quality relative to expectation – behind Jude and Morgan Rogers.

Jobe is fourth for pressured passes, too, with Jude in second, as they've both picked up a similar level of press resistance from those years of development in the Bundesliga. But it's defensively that they're most similar.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Jude is in the 95th percentile for duel-winning across Europe, with Jobe in the 77th. The Bellingham brothers top our prospective magnificent seven, with Eze lagging behind in third – and in 1v1 defending, Jude again leads, with Jobe in second.

Across the board, Rogers is still the closest to Jude Bellingham in terms of all-round game. When it comes to tackle resistance, Jude leads the group with a score of 92.6 on the scale, but Rogers is the next closest at 82.6. By comparison, Jobe is at 76.1, and players like Eze (64.4) and Palmer (70.6) fall far behind. Rogers is also the clear runner-up in both On-Ball Attacking (78.6) and Open Play (75.1) categories, with Jobe scoring much lower here (65.7 and 69.6, respectively).

While Jobe lacks Jude’s elite attacking output and ball retention, he manages to match Jude's defensive and out-of-possession numbers reasonably well. Incidentally, fellow first-time call-up Josh King ranks well for both duels and ball-carrying – finding himself even ahead of Jude.

The Bellingham brothers' continued rise and the inclusion of talents like Gibbs-White and King point to a change in tack from manager Thomas Tuchel. Both Phil Foden and Cole Palmer have enjoyed clamour from fans for them to both start for England in the past – but the German resisted taking either to the World Cup.

And digging into the data, both of them represent hugely different profiles to their contemporaries. Palmer offers elite passing and carrying, actually beating Jude in Ball Carrying (79.5 vs Jude's 67.6) and Through Balls (83.7 vs Jude's 77.8). However, he is a poor stylistic replacement for Jude in physical midfield battles, scoring the lowest of the group in All Duels (53.7 vs Jude's 76.0). Foden rates significantly lower than Jude in physical areas like Tackle Resistance (71.5) and 1v1 Defending (64.4), too, perhaps indicating why he's seldom been used centrally for his country.

They're both elite players on their day: more technical and pass-heavy, but less robust in physical duels – and including players for their technical prowess while ignoring defensive limitations seems to be something of the past now, even at international level. A move towards Spain-like schemers that began with the Elite Player Performance Plan in 2012 really is old news now and this confirms it.

Mark White has been at on FourFourTwo since joining in January 2020, first as a staff writer before becoming content editor in 2023. An encyclopedia of football shirts and boots knowledge – both past and present – Mark has also represented FFT at both FA Cup and League Cup finals (though didn't receive a winners' medal on either occasion) and has written pieces for the mag ranging on subjects from Bobby Robson's season at Barcelona to Robinho's career. He has written cover features for the mag on Mikel Arteta and Martin Odegaard, and is assisted by his cat, Rosie, who has interned for the brand since lockdown.

#1023. Andy Robertson wants equalling Scotland caps record to be Kenny Dalglish tribute

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Andy Robertson believes reaching his 102nd international cap should serve as an opportunity to celebrate Sir Kenny Dalglish rather than focus on himself, as he prepares to equal the record held by his fellow former Liverpool player.

The 32-year-old will draw level with Dalglish when he captains Scotland at Hampden against North Macedonia in Friday's Nations League match.

"Tomorrow’s not really about me," the Tottenham left-back said. "It’s about him in my opinion. For how long the record stood, for what he achieved in his career, for the person he is.

"It’s another reason for our country to tip our hat to one of the greatest players that have played the game, never mind in Scotland, he’s definitely the greatest in Scotland."

Robertson spoke on the 40th anniversary of Dalglish’s final match for Scotland, a 3-0 victory against Luxembourg delivered during his second season operating as Liverpool player/manager.

"That tells you everything that you need to know, the fact that he’s juggling all that and still showing up for his country," Robertson said.

"He reminds me all the time that 102 caps back then was a lot harder than 102 caps now, and he’s right because there were less games.

"In terms of numbers, I’ll stand side by side with him, but I don’t want people to forget how important this man has been for our country.

"He was arguably the best player in the world at his time and he’ll always be the greatest in this country."

Dalglish recently joked that he hoped Robertson would hang up his boots before establishing a new record.

"We’ve had a lot of jokes, but I also know deep down how proud he is of me and how happy he is for me as well," the former Dundee United player said.

"I always remember when I got the captaincy, he was one of the first people to text me and say, ‘I know I’ve been out of the game maybe a little bit, but if you need help, if you need somebody to bounce anything off, then I can be that person’.

"To have somebody like that, that you can bounce anything off and rely on, him and his family have been such a massive help to my family, especially in my time at Liverpool.

"I’ve got no doubt there’ll be a couple of texts that will get exchanged. I know we laugh and we joke, publicly and privately, but I know he’s proud of me and he’s happy for what I’ve achieved as well."

Robertson is expected to surpass Dalglish in Switzerland on Monday, and he shows no signs of slowing down.

"I’m still hungry to achieve more for the country," he said. "I want to get Scotland back to another major tournament, I want to try and get out the group stages.

"Secondly, I want to try and leave the squad in the best possible place in terms of the quality coming through, the characters they’ve got, the mentality they’ve got.

"If I can leave that behind, then I can maybe enjoy Scotland games a bit more and I can join the fans and party with them."
