#887. League One clubs aim for further curbs on spending as budgets continue to spiral

Wage bills in third tier have increased by 15% this season

‘Luxury tax’ and three-year limits on losses considered

League One clubs want to introduce new spending restrictions to reduce losses by limiting investment from owners.

Clubs in the division voted to tighten the rules last summer by reducing spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover, and removed a staggered approach to owner investment, so that only 50% of equity injections can be spent on squad costs, with the rest assigned to infrastructure projects. Less than six months later many want to go further.

The Guardian has learned that two proposed models are being ­con­sidered: a fixed cap on owner investment or introducing a version of the Premier League’s squad cost rules, with a £1 levy on clubs for every £1 spent above 50% of their revenue. Sporting sanctions would be applied if spending reached 60%, with the money raised from the levy redistri­buted to other clubs in the division.

The move to introduce more spending curbs comes despite a legal challenge to the existing rules from the Professional ­Footballers’ Association, which launched proceedings in August on the grounds that the clubs had failed to abide by the terms of their membership of the ­professional negotiating and consultative committee.

An attempt by League One and League Two to introduce salary caps of £2.5m and £1.5m respectively was withdrawn in 2021 after the PFA took them to an independent arbitration panel.

Discussions over stricter controls have been taking place for some time, but have been given fresh impetus by the publication last month of the State of the Game report. The first piece of work by the ­Independent Football Regulator showed that 94% of clubs in the EFL and National League are loss-making, and that 32 of the 96 would not survive for a month without owner funding.

The changes last summer reduced the percentage of clubs’ income that can be spent on wages, with mana­gers’ salaries included for the first time, but there is a renewed move to reduce losses, which averaged £7.5m per club in League One last season, up from £5.3m the previous season.

One owner said that further regulation was ­necessary because the clubs had shown ­repeatedly that they could not restrain themselves, pointing out that League One wage bills have increased by 15% this season, and that a top-six budget in the division five years ago would now rank in the bottom three.

Reading and Peterborough have long campaigned for tighter spending controls, but face opposition from clubs such as MK Dons and Wycombe, and it is unclear whether any proposal would gain the two-thirds majority required to be introduced.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

A source at another League One club warned that an unintended consequence would be to create a cliff edge in terms of financial resources with the Championship, which loosened its regulations last season by permitting owners an inject up to £33m over three years, an equity allowance that does not count towards the 85% wage spending/revenue limit.

League Two clubs are also involved in the discussions, although it is unclear whether they will choose to align with League One.

The EFL confirmed discussions were ongoing, although formal proposals have yet to be put to the clubs.

#886. Kane the hero on historic night as England book Nations League QF spot

England vs Croatia. UEFA Nations League Group A3.

Match report from Wembley as Harry Kane marks his 126th England cap with the winner from the penalty spot; Morgan Rogers bundled opener but Three Lions needed Kane to convert after Jarell Quansah's error allowed Croatia to level; England into Nations League quarter-finals

Senior Football Journalist @psmithXI

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Record-breaker Harry Kane scored from the spot to seal England's place in the Nations League quarter-finals with a 2-1 victory over Croatia, capping a memorable Wembley night as the captain became his country's most-capped player.

There was an inevitability about Kane hitting the net on his 126th appearance. There had been pre-match tributes and accolades as the Ballon d'Or holder passed the mark of legendary goalkeeper Peter Shilton and once again Kane was England's match winner with his second-half spot-kick. That's 92 goals now in England colours for the record scorer.

The win means England will now have the chance to win Nations League Group A3 and be seeded for the quarter-finals - but they will have to be far better than this if they are to beat table-toppers and world champions Spain in Madrid on Sunday.

The Nations League quarter-finals will take place in March, with the top two from each League A group going into the draw.Teams which finish top of their group will be seeded and drawn against teams which have finished second for the two-leg ties which will determine who make it into the Nations League finals in June.

England thumped Croatia 7-0 last month but this was a performance far shy of that previous display, lacking intensity and final-third spark for long periods, and littered with jittery moments at the back.

Thankfully for Thomas Tuchel, he has Kane. The captain orchestrated the opener in his trademark style, dropping deep before clipping a fine pass for Jude Bellingham to cross for Morgan Rogers to bundle in when Josko Gvardiol failed to clear.

But moments after Kane's Bayern Munich team-mate Josip Stansic made a key block on the England skipper, Jarell Quansah's blunder gave Croatia a gift. His header back to Jordan Pickford was too casual and pounced on by Petar Sucic.

Quansah almost immediately made amends, being hauled down from an England corner by Ivan Smolcic for Kane to have his big moment.

But still England couldn't go up through the gears. James Garner's celebrations were cut short by an offside flag but the final stages were nervy for the hosts, with Nikola Vlasic wastefully clipping wide and Ante Budimir heading over.

On Kane's historic night, England were again indebted to their captain fantastic.

"It was an okay performance overall. It took us a while to figure the press out because they played in a back five. It needed a lot of communication because we wanted to stay in our structure.

"Once we figured that out after 15 minutes we were the better team. You felt the confidence coming. We got a bit sloppy in the last five minutes of the first half. Good reaction at the start of the second half. Created more and more.

"We got again sloppy for five minutes and were punished from a set-piece which is uncharacteristic from us. Then we needed to show a reaction because we were desperate for a result.

"Croatia had nothing to lose and you have to overcome these moments."

"It was incredible. Everything was amazing. Thank you to everyone who organised [the build-up], with the tifo and presentations. Thank you to Luka [Modric] and Croatia for their gift.

"I knew there would be something before the game. It's been a crazy few weeks with a lot happening, but it's an important moment in our history as a national team.

"But once the game started it was full focus. These occasions feel much better when you win and now I can take a breath and enjoy this."

15: CLOSE! Elliot Anderson goes close to his first England goal with a decent snapshot from 20 yards.

18: BLOCK! A Bellingham cross is cleared as far as Trent Alexander-Arnold, who strikes it well but into the body of Josip Misic.

24: GOAL! Kane's fine pass into the box finds Bellingham to volley a cross for Rogers to bundle in.

48: WIDE! Anthony Gordon takes aim but doesn't get the bend on his shot he'd like and it flies well wide.

51: BIG BLOCK! Kane is denied a goal when his Bayern Munich team-mate Stanisic gets in the way as the England captain tries to turn in Declan Rice's cutback.

55: PENALTY APPEALS! But there's deemed to be no foul when Gordon is bundled over by Misic before Bellingham hits the target with a follow-up shot.

59: GOAL! Quansah tries to head the ball back to Jordan Pickford from a Croatia corner but Sucic is there to pounce and poke in. A bad mistake from the England centre-back!

63: PENALTY TO ENGLAND! After a VAR check referee Morten Krogh awards England a penalty for Quansah being pulled down from an England corner by Smolcic.

64: GOAL! Record-breaker Kane scores from the spot for England goal number 92.

82: BIG CHANCE! But Vlasic clips his shot wide when he looked set to equalise.

86: NO GOAL! Garner is denied his first England goal by the offside flag.

88: BLOCK! Quansah slides in to block Budimir's shot.

90+2: CHANCE! But Budimir heads over from a late corner.

Sky Sports News' Rob Dorsett at Wembley Stadium:

"As a game, it was instantly forgettable. As an occasion, it will live long in the memory. But that is all about what happened pre-match, rather than during the 90 minutes.

"Captain Kane being recognised as not only the best player in the world, but also as England's most capped player of all time, was a proper "I was there" moment. Inevitably, he scored to mark the occasion, with a coolly-slotted second-half penalty.

"But beyond that, England were disappointing. Flat. Lifeless, in the main. Lacking energy, spark and invention. The two full-backs, Alexander-Arnold and Hall, came out of it with some credit. And Elliot Anderson was as industrious and effective as ever. But that was about it.

"It was enough to ensure a victory - just about - and to set up a winner-takes-all Nations League group finale against the world champions Spain in Madrid on Sunday. Maybe England's players had that game in the back of their minds, and held back a bit. Let's hope that's what it was, anyway."

James was on the scoresheet as Wales came from behind to see off the World Cup quarter-finalists, reigniting hopes of staying in the top tier of the Nations League.

It represented the biggest scalp of Bellamy's reign, ending a winless run of six and quietening some of the rumblings of discontent around the manager.

Repeating the trick in Oslo on Saturday (17:00 GMT) would inch Wales to within a whisker of securing third spot and the boost to Euro 2028 qualifying seedings that comes with it.

In contrast, Norway are on their worst run of form in a decade and in danger of dropping out of the European elite they seemed on course to challenge.

Wales boss Bellamy praises Liverpool's handling of Koumas

Johnson says definitely more to come after 50 caps

Norwegian media were critical of the side that lost in Cardiff having also been beaten in games against Portugal immediately before and after.

The defeat in Oslo â in which Cristiano Ronaldo was left on the bench by Portugal, prompting his walk out and eventual international retirement â was the first time Norway had lost in 12 competitive matches at home.

And Norway have not lost four games in a row since 2016, well before the emergence of much of their current golden generation.

#883. US withdraw from U-17 World Cup in Qatar due to safety concerns

USSF cites state department advisory about Qatar

Competition set to kick off in eight days

The US men’s national team have pulled out of the Fifa U-17 World Cup, which is due to kick off in Qatar in just over a week. In a letter sent to players explaining the decision, the US Soccer Federation cited safety concerns for players and staff, referring them to the US state department’s travel advisory for Qatar, which encourages citizens to reconsider travel to the country “due to risk of armed conflict” and asks government employees to obtain special authorization to do so.

“Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances … we are no longer able to participate in the tournament,” US Soccer’s letter to players reads. “The wellbeing of our players and staff will always be our top priority.

“Please accept our deepest appreciation for your commitment to US Soccer and our shared disappointment about these circumstances.”

A US Soccer spokesperson said the federation would not go into details about how it reached its decision. The Guardian understands Fifa was informed of the federation’s decision on Wednesday.

Fifa’s regulations for the U-17 World Cups stipulate that qualified nations must participate in the tournament or be fined, with withdrawal within 30 days of the tournament’s start resulting in a fine of CHF20,000 (about $24,000).

“Fifa has been informed of US Soccer’s decision to withdraw from the Fifa U-17 World Cup Qatar 2026,” Fifa told the Guardian in a statement. “The applicable tournament regulations will be followed. Fifa’s security assessments remain unchanged, and no new developments affecting the security situation around the tournament have occurred. Fifa understands that US Soccer’s decision was made in light of the existing US Level 3 travel advisory.”

The ongoing situation in the Middle East – involving interconnected conflicts among multiple states – has already led to postponements or cancellations of international sporting events. The 2027 Asian Cup, the continental soccer championship, was due to be held in Saudi Arabia in January 2027 but has been postponed nearly a year due to the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthi rebels, and the Iran war. More recently, Qatar pulled out of hosting rugby’s 2028 Nations Championship finals due to uncertainty around the conflicts. The final races of the Formula One season are still going ahead in the Middle East, on 29 November in Qatar and then 6 December in Abu Dhabi.

Fifa told the Guardian it had taken the situation in the Middle East into account.

“The safety and security of all participants and fans remains paramount,” Fifa said in its statement. “As with all Fifa tournaments and events, we are in close contact with the relevant authorities and are looking forward to the tournament kick-off in Qatar. In recent months, Qatar has successfully hosted several international events, including the FIP Padel World Cup, the FIVB Volleyball Boys’ U17 World Championship, the Doha Diamond League, the Fiba Basketball World Cup 2027 Asian Qualifiers, the MotoGP and the UN ITU PP.”

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Multiple missile strikes by the Houthis on Riyadh’s international airport killed 13 people and wounded hundreds in October. Later that month, US diplomats were told to leave Saudi Arabia amid ongoing Houthi attacks.

Qatar has been acting as a mediator in talks between the US and Iran aimed at ending the countries’ conflict, which started with attacks by the US and Israel on Iran earlier this year. A tanker off the coast of Qatar was attacked in October amid thetensions.

The U-17 World Cup is still due to begin on 19 November in Doha. The US were placed in Group J along with Montenegro, Algeria and Chile. The US roster that was due to compete in the tournament does not contain any household names, but features a number of promising young players in MLS and abroad.

#882. Efficient catalyst-controlled C–H arylation of arenes

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Direct arylation of C–H bonds in arenes offers a streamlined alternative to widely used cross-coupling reactions.1 However, native substrates lack the preinstalled functional handles that ordinarily provide both reactivity and control over the site of reaction. Consequently, despite long-standing interest in directly engaging C–H bonds as reactive sites,2–4 the design of general catalysts that deliver high yields across diverse substrate classes while controlling site selectivity remains a challenge.5–12 Here we show that a microenvironment around a prototypical palladium dicarboxylate catalytic site can provide high selectivity for direct arylation of sterically exposed C–H sites, while high efficiency is achieved using an advanced palladium(II) precatalyst and tailored diaryliodonium reagents for selective aryl transfer. The applicability of this system spans from electron-rich to electron-deficient arenes, while electron-neutral benzene, which is often a challenge for C–H arylation, undergoes successive sterically controlled arylations, delivering functionalized polyaryl compounds. In addition to removing the necessity for pre-functionalized substrates, the mild conditions enable direct late-stage C–H arylation and the installation of aryl groups equipped with functionalities that are typically either reactive in traditional cross-coupling catalysis, such as triflates, iodides, and boronate esters, or sensitive to the basic conditions, such as N-hydroxysuccinimide esters. The results emphasize the distinct synthetic value of palladium-catalyzed direct C–H arylation reactions and showcase a catalyst platform that facilitates high yields and control over site-selectivity.

#881. How 'Barca way' continues despite big-name exits

Esmee Brugts has made more than 100 appearances for Barcelona after joining in 2023

Barcelona's team is markedly different to the one Arsenal faced in the 2025 Women's Champions League final - but the challenge is as difficult as ever.

Three-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas was among a number of high-profile summer departures, but Barca remain favourites to continue their European domination.

The reigning champions have won all three league-phase matches, scoring 19 goals, and welcome Arsenal to the Nou Camp on Thursday (17:45 GMT).

Two seasons ago, Arsenal stunned Barcelona in the Women's Champions League final, less than five months after Renee Slegers was named permanent manager.

That victory kick-started a new era for the Gunners under Slegers, but it has not gone to plan so far this season.

Disappointing results and a five-game winless run, which ended in October, have left Arsenal sixth in the Women's Super League.

However, the Gunners have started the European campaign well and are fifth in the table with seven points from their first three matches.

And given Barcelona's summer changes, Arsenal might have hoped to be facing a team in transition - but the Spanish giants look as strong as ever.

So how have Barca - who have won four of the past six Women's Champions League titles - hit the ground running this term despite losing some of their key players?

Nations League draw, BBC Womenâs Footballer of the Year & can Arsenal shock Barcelona again?

Cast your vote for BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026

What is the Women's Champions League prize money?

When Spain great Putellas left Barcelona in the summer to join London City Lionesses, it felt like the end of an era.

She was followed to Bromley by defender Mapi Leon, while full-back Ona Batlle joined Arsenal and Salma Paralluelo swapped Barcelona for European rivals Lyon.

All four had played a key part in Barcelona's dominance and ended their time at the club with a historic quadruple, including a fourth Champions League last season.

So how have Barcelona coped with losing such big players?

"Every season is different. There are always changes but we know that's football," Barcelona's Esmee Brugts told BBC Sport.

"There's an opportunity to make a new story and that's up to us. So far, I've been quite happy with how it's going.

"I'm excited for the upcoming games to see how we do. It can be a bit different - but different in a good way also."

Barcelona's success is down to multiple factors, but it all centres around a distinctive playing identity that is ingrained in Spanish footballers from a young age.

Stars such as three-time Ballon d'Or winner Aitana Bonmati were developed at the club's famous La Masia youth academy, situated next to the Estadi Johan Cruyff, which is named after one of Barca's greatest footballers.

They produce a conveyor belt of talent, all trained to play the same way, and having learned to swap in and out of positions seamlessly.

It is a way of playing that Netherlands international Brugts has picked up with ease since joining in 2023.

"It's difficult to explain because it's so many small things. It's doing the simple things good," said Brugts. "It's a team sport. If everybody does their own roles, you'll perform the best way.

"I watched a documentary about Johan Cruyff and it's exactly how he wanted to play. It's how we try to play every week. We try to be as perfect as possible.

"We try to win every trophy there is by playing really beautiful football, in my opinion. The 'tiki-taka' I enjoy so much."

Barcelona beat rivals Real Madrid 7-0 last month in Liga F

Arsenal boss Slegers said Barcelona have "a really strong identity" and she does not believe this changes when new players come into the side.

"They can play in different positions and also have a very strong and clear way of playing. It's very impressive with the way Barcelona plays," said Slegers.

"With new players coming in and then rotating, their style of play stands up. We think we have quite a clear idea of what that could look like."

While it is a new era for Barcelona, their ambitions remain the same - to defend their four titles this season.

Brugts said they are "really building" their identity with new players in the squad and believe there are "no limits" to what they can produce.

Talented youngsters such as midfielder Clara Serrajordi, 18, defender Renee van Asten, 20, and forward Vicky Lopez, 20, have added more depth to the squad.

"It took me some time to adjust, to learn and understand what it is to play the Barca way. I'm still not there, but it's a process," said 23-year-old Brugts.

"It's an interesting journey - to do it surrounded by the best players, some that have left and some that are still here.

"I'm super-grateful and I'm super-proud if I look at what's coming up from the younger teams. I'm very impressed with how good they are.

"The way Barcelona plays is something you have to learn when you are young. Whenever we need them, they are ready to play and understand the game."

#880. Danny Kelly, football broadcaster and renowned editor, dies aged 69

Danny Baker pays tribute to the ‘funniest man I knew’

Kelly was former editor of the NME and Q magazines

The journalist and broadcaster Danny Kelly, who helped define coverage of music and football in the UK for a generation, has died at the age of 69.

Kelly edited the NME and Q magazine, and launched the Football 365 website before going on to be a presenter and pundit on the BBC and TalkSport. He had been receiving treatment for oesophageal cancer.

Tributes were led by Kelly’s longstanding broadcast partner Danny Baker. “My great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew, Danny Kelly, died yesterday afternoon,” Baker wrote on social media, the pair having worked together on any number of radio, TV shows and podcasts. “I cannot believe I will never hear his voice again.”

Tottenham Hotspur paid emotional tribute to Kelly, a lifelong Spurs fan. A statement said: “The entire Tottenham family mourns the loss of one of our own, broadcasting legend Danny Kelly. Our thoughts and love are with his family and friends at this incredibly sad time.”

TalkSport, for which Kelly worked as a presenter for nearly two decades, said it was “heartbroken” by the news. “A cherished part of TalkSport for so many years, Danny brought extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves,” the station said. “His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him.”

Another broadcaster, the former Sky Sports host Richard Keys, said Kelly “was all of the things – and more – being said about him – ‘warm, witty and knowledgable’”.

Kelly was born in north London in 1956 and first made his name writing about music. He began contributing to the NME in his 20s and went on to edit the agenda-setting weekly newspaper at the end of the 1980s. From there he took charge of the top-selling music monthly Q magazine, where he was named British magazine editor of the year.

Manic Street Preachers paid tribute to “a brilliant broadcaster-writer-ideas factory. Danny was editor of the NME when we first started getting press, a wonderful man, his musical knowledge was vast and deep, his radio voice has been part of our lives for so long … We will all miss him.”

In the second half of the 1990s, Kelly threw himself into the nascent world of digital media and launched Football365, which became one of the leading online voices on the sport. In the noughties, he spotted another development – podcasts – and launched the Game, a weekly football podcast, for the Times.

Over the past 15 years Kelly became best known as a radio presenter and podcast host, including presenting the Tottenham-focused show View from The Lane. Paying tribute to “our host, our leader” on its X account, the View from the Lane said: “We all loved him as much as he loved Spurs.”

The top stories and transfer rumours from Friday's newspapers...

#877. Complaint filed to IRS in relation to Fifa head Gianni Infantino’s housekeeper

It calls for inquiry into claims she was on Fifa payroll

Fifa: Infantino personally pays for ‘any domestic staff’

A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for an investigation into claims an individual on the Fifa payroll was working privately as a housekeeper for Gianni Infantino.

If the IRS investigates and finds the claims to be proven then Fifa could lose its tax-exempt status in the US. Fifa has 501(c)(4) status in the country, a category for organisations “created to promote community welfare for charitable, educational or recreational purposes”.

The complaint, which has been seen by the Guardian and is supported by a number of documents, claims an individual “performed domestic work exclusively for Fifa president Gianni Infantino and his wife, Leena Infantino, at their Miami residence, while receiving compensation or benefits through a Fifa-affiliated entity”, and argues that “senior leadership, acting in their official capacity and on behalf of Fifa, have abused the entity’s tax-exemption status”.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

The complaint goes on to argue: “If organisational funds or resources were used to pay for services benefiting a leader’s household, the arrangement raises serious questions about private benefit, financial reporting, compensation, and governance. The materials also raise questions about the accuracy of representations in employment, payroll, tax, and immigration records. We ask the agencies to investigate the underlying records and determine what occurred.” The IRS has been approached for comment.

The news comes as Fifa’s activities, and specifically Infantino’s involvement in the failed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme and his relationship with the Trump White House, are to come under intensified scrutiny from Democratic politicians in the US after the “blue wave” at the midterm elections. A spokesperson for the ranking member of the House judiciary committee, representative Jamie Raskin, said the committee had not requested documents related to the housekeeper but was “looking closely at those developments”.

A Fifa spokesperson said: “Matters related to the Fifa president’s personal and home life are private; however, for the avoidance of any doubt, the costs of any domestic staff are met by the Fifa president personally.”

The complaint, if taken up, would probably take months to complete and commonly the results of IRS investigations are not published. Any action taken as a result, however, would be in the public domain. The complaint was submitted by the Washington DC lawyer Abed Ayoub, who works in immigration law and has served as the national executive director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC). Last year the ADC was part of the campaign Game Over Israel, which called for Israeli football teams to be banned from international competition.

Fifa said: “We urge the media to act responsibly. As Fifa stated in August, it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president. Fifa welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to amplify false allegations. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading Fifa will continue to challenge it directly and vigorously.”

Infantino has been described by his predecessor, Sepp Blatter, as a “dictator” who “no longer knows any borders”. Blatter, Fifa’s president for 17 years before resigning amid a corruption scandal at the organisation, made the remarks in an interview with the German magazine Der Spiegel. He criticised the FFE scheme, the Fifa peace prize and, most significantly in his opinion, the overturning of Folarin Balogun’s suspension for a red card during the World Cup.

Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in

“Fifa is suffering,” Blatter said. “It is currently led by a person who has allowed himself to be blinded.” He described the peace prize as “embarrassing”, saying: “Why would he do something like that? Infantino awards a peace prize to someone who wages war against Iran shortly afterwards?”

In assessing the FFE scheme, which was abandoned after an international outcry, Blatter said: “Infantino no longer knows any borders. He doesn’t understand any of this.” He described the Balogun controversy as “the worst”, saying: “Statutes can be interpreted. But rules of the game must apply to everyone, you can’t interpret them.”

#876. Pochettino agrees two-and-a-half-year deal to become Man Utd boss

Mauricio Pochettino will take charge of Manchester United after the current international break; USA boss will replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday with the club in the Premier League relegation zone; Pochettino will sign deal until summer of 2029

Manchester United and Mauricio Pochettino have agreed a deal for him to become the club's next head coach.

Pochettino is expected to sign a two-and-half-year contract at Old Trafford, replacing Michael Carrick, who was sacked earlier on Thursday.

Pochettino - who had a £7m release clause in his USA contract - will take charge of United after overseeing the USA's games against Haiti on Saturday and Wednesday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The formal announcement of Pochettino's appointed is expected on Friday, with the Argentine set to be United's eighth permanent appointment since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

Pochettino's first game in charge will be the trip to Anfield to face Liverpool on November 22, live on Sky Sports.

Carrick departed less than six months after signing a two-year contract having overseen the club's worst start to a Premier League season, with United in the relegation zone after picking up one win in 10 matches.

In a statement on Thursday morning, shortly after Carrick left the training ground, United said they reached "the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions".

Carrick took training in Manchester on Wednesday as United reached a verbal agreement with Pochettino.

Meanwhile, club chiefs were at a Monaco summit with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe. That is where the decision to sack Carrick was ratified by Ratcliffe following the recommendation of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

United's hierarchy, including Wilcox and Berrada, are understood to feel that the current squad is much better than results and performances have shown.

Carrick's exit follows United's 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on Sunday, when they fell 2-0 down inside four minutes and then 4-2 down early in the second half before mounting a last-gasp comeback to draw.

The rescue job followed a similar turnaround to beat Roma in the Champions League last Tuesday but was not enough to convince the United hierarchy to continue with the former midfielder in charge.

Jonny Evans and Jonathan Woodgate, who were part of the coaching set up under Carrick, have also left the club, along with Steve Holland, Travis Binnion and goalkeeping coach Craig Mawson.

The only coach who remains is assistant first-team goalkeeping coach Connor King, who joined the club two months ago.

Carrick was initially appointed as United boss in January 2026 on a contract until the end of the season following Ruben Amorim's sacking earlier in that campaign. He delivered a brilliant run of results, winning 12 of 17 matches to earn a third-place finish in the Premier League and a return to the Champions League.

Carrick was nominated for Premier League Manager of the Season and, on May 22, signed a new contract running to 2028. However, just three wins in 15 matches this term have cost him his job.

Former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain boss Pochettino has been considered for the United job on three previous occasions, but will now finally take the Old Trafford hot seat.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"You can keep changing the manager and thinking that's going to be the answer. But this has been proven now over 12 years, that's not the answer.

"It's rinse and repeat. Ruben Amorim, Erik ten Hag, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Carrick, Jose Mourinho, Louis van Gaal, David Moyes, Ralf Rangnick - some of them are world-class managers who have had success. There are a lot of promising young managers there, ex-players who know the club as well.

"None of it has worked because if you've got a poor performance department, poor recruitment department, you've not got leadership that is strong right through the spine of the football club, you will fail."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

United won 12 out of 17 games last season under Carrick - a 70.1 per cent win rate, which saw him comfortably sit with the best record of permanent Old Trafford managers.

But he leaves with a record of 15 wins in 32 matches - a rate of just 46.9 per cent, which leaves him only ahead of Ruben Amorim, the man he replaced in the dugout last season, in the years since Ferguson's retirement.

Carrick has overseen three wins in 15 matches this campaign (20 per cent). They won eight out of 21 games before Amorim's sacking last year (38.1 per cent).

His drop-off brings echoes of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer. The former United striker's win percentage fell from 73.7 per cent as interim manager (14 wins in 19 games) to 51.7 per cent having been appointed on a permanent basis (77 out of 149).

Carrick had three games as caretaker boss after Solskjaer's departure, wins over Villarreal and Arsenal and a draw with Chelsea. These matches are not counted towards his record as permanent manager.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Since the retirement in 2013 of Ferguson, who won 26 major trophies in 27 years at Old Trafford and had a 59.7 per cent win ratio, United have struggled to find a long-term figurehead.

Ferguson took charge of 1,500 games with United. In 731 games since he retired in 2013, Carrick was the club's seventh permanent manager in addition to interim boss Ralf Rangnick and caretakers Ryan Giggs, Carrick himself, Ruud van Nistelrooy and Darren Fletcher.

Jose Mourinho has the best win percentage of those permanent managers, with 58.3 per cent, 84 out of 144 games.

Mourinho also won the most trophies of any manager since Ferguson, with a League Cup and Europa League double in 2016-17 having opened that season with the Community Shield.

Erik ten Hag won both domestic cups, Louis van Gaal lifted an FA Cup and David Moyes another Community Shield.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

December 2023: Sir Jim Ratcliffe's deal to purchase a stake in United is announced.

January 2024: United appoint Omar Berrada from rivals Manchester City as their new chief executive. The move was made by Ratcliffe in consultation with Joel and Avram Glazer but INEOS were the driving force behind the move.

February 2024: Ratcliffe completes deal to acquire 27.7 per cent stake in Manchester United, which gives his company, INEOS, control of football operations.

April 2024: INEOS and Ratcliffe shake-up continued as United appoint Jason Wilcox as technical director after less than a year as director of football at Southampton, which was his first executive role in senior football.

July 2024: Man Utd agree deal with Newcastle United to appoint Dan Ashworth as sporting director after a lengthy period of gardening leave.

July 2024: Erik ten Hag is handed a one-year contract extension after winning the FA Cup by beating Manchester City 2-1 in the final. He is backed with the signings of Matthijs De Ligt, Noussair Mazraoui, Joshua Zirkzee, Manuel Ugarte and Leny Yoro.

July 2024: Christopher Vivell is hired as director of global talent on a temporary basis.

October 2024: United sack manager Ten Hag after winning just four of their 14 games to start the 2024/25 season. United in 14th and Ruud van Nistelrooy appointed as interim boss.

November 2024: Ruben Amorim is confirmed as the club's new head coach, signing a contract until June 2027. United paid £9.2m to release him from Sporting.

December 2024: Ashworth leaves his role as sporting director after just five months. He oversaw a £200m spend in the transfer market.

December 2024: Wilcox steps into Ashworth's role as sporting director.

February 2025: Vivell is appointed as permanent director of recruitment.

June 2025: Wilcox is promoted to director of football after Sir Dave Brailsford ends association with the club. He is tasked with overseeing football operations, including recruitment.

January 5 2026: Amorim is sacked after 14 months in charge after winning only 24 of his 63 games in charge. Darren Fletcher is appointed as interim boss.

January 13 2026: Michael Carrick is appointed as head coach until the end of the 2025/26 season.

May 2026: After securing Champions League football and winning 12 of his 17 games in charge, Carrick is rewarded with a two-year deal at Old Trafford.

November 12 2026: Carrick leaves United following a draw with Aston Villa, which left the club in the Premier League relegation zone after 10 games.

Michael Carrick has been sacked as Manchester United head coach, so how did his Old Trafford reign go so wrong, so quickly?

The former midfielder guided United to a Champions League finish last season but after their worst start to a season in 40 years, they are in the Premier League relegation zone at the start of November.

United salvaged a 4-4 draw against Aston Villa in Carrick's final game in charge, but they have only won once in 10 Premier League fixtures so far despite finishing last term on a high, with former Spurs and Chelsea boss Mauricio Pochettino set to take over.

#874. Actress Lisa Maxwell’s Daughter Beau Jessup Dies at 27

Beau Jessup, the only child of British actress Lisa Maxwell and her husband Paul Jessup, died at the age of 27 while studying journalism at Columbia University in New York, according to her school.

Lisa Maxwell’s family is grieving a tragic loss.

Beau Jessup—the daughter of the British TV actress and her husband Paul Jessup—died at the age of 27, according to Columbia Journalism School, where Jessup was studying as a graduate student.

“Columbia Journalism School mourns the loss of Beau Jessup, a student in our M.S. program,” the school shared in a Nov. 9 statement. “We extend our deepest condolences to her family, friends, classmates and all who knew and loved her.”

Before her death, Jessup gave an interview with her college paper Columbia News in which she detailed how Maxwell—known for her role as Samantha Nixon on The Bill from 2001 to 2009 and as a presenter on the chat show Loose Women—inspired her to pursue journalism.

“As the daughter of a television actress, I grew up with an unusual awareness of the distance between people’s lives and the stories told about them,” she shared in the interview published Nov. 9. “I saw how journalism could illuminate someone’s experiences, but also how those experiences could be distorted, simplified, or transformed into a public narrative over which the subject had very little control.”

She added, “I was curious, from quite a young age, about who gets to tell people’s stories, and what happens when those stories enter the public domain.”

Plus, Jessup—who previously earned a master’s degree in Writing for Performance at the University of Cambridge—used her life’s experiences to understand “the power and the responsibility of storytelling.”

As for what she planned to do upon graduating in May?

“I want to work as a journalist and writer, reporting on people, culture, and social questions with the rigor I’m learning at Columbia,” Jessup said. “I’m particularly drawn to journalism for its power and immediacy, while continuing to write for theater when a subject benefits from being explored through a different form.”

Jessup was also interested in continuing her creative writing, hoping to have her work reach new heights.

“While completing my Master’s in Writing for Performance at the University of Cambridge, I wrote my first play, The Sandbag,” she added. “If I can arrange a table reading of The Sandbag in Pulitzer Hall [on campus], I’ll technically be able to claim my first play was performed on Broadway. Geographically speaking, at least.”

As for Maxwell—who also voiced Kira in Jim Henson and Frank Oz’s 1982 hit movie The Dark Crystal—her career turned to soap operas after she left The Bill in 2009, as she went on to star in Hollyoaks from 2016 to 2017.

Jordan Ayew joined Championship side Sheffield United in September after spending two seasons with Leicester City

Ghana belatedly kick-started their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifying campaign with a 2-0 home win over Somalia.

The Black Stars had lost their opening two Group C matches against Ivory Coast and The Gambia, leading to the departure of coach Carlos Queiroz by mutual consent.

Ghana women's coach Kim Bjorkegren was placed in interim charge for this month's double-header against the Ocean Stars, with the West Africans in danger of missing a second successive edition of the Afcon finals.

The hosts were given a chance to take an early lead in Sekondi-Takoradi after Alidu Seidu was pulled down in the box, but Jordan Ayew's 14th-minute penalty was saved by Somalia goalkeeper Ibrahim Hussein.

Ghana did go ahead in first-half stoppage time when Mohammed Salisu headed Mohammed Kudus's deep corner back across goal and Jonas Adjetey nodded in from six yards out.

Felix Afena-Gyan doubled the Black Stars' advantage just after the hour mark when his shot from inside the box squirmed under Hussein and over the line.

The four-time continental champions remain six points behind group leaders Ivory Coast, who extended their 100% record by beating The Gambia 2-1 in Bouake.

Brighton midfielder Malick Yalcouye tucked in from seven yards out and Elye Wahi slotted home to double the Elephants' lead before Musa Barrow pulled one back for the visitors before the break.

Elsewhere on Thursday, there were wins for Cameroon, DR Congo and Senegal, who all remain on track to qualify for next year's tournament in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

The third round of qualifying fixtures continues on Friday with Egypt, Morocco, Nigeria and South Africa in action among 12 fixtures.

Nicolas Jackson has 11 goals in 17 appearances for club and country this season

Nicolas Jackson set Senegal on their way to a 4-1 home win over Sudan in Group J, with Aston Villa team-mate Ibrahim Mbaye also on the scoresheet for Patrick Vieira's men in Dakar.

The Teranga Lions lead the standings on seven points, three ahead of Mozambique, who host Ethiopia on Friday.

Cameroon also remained unbeaten and moved on to seven points in Group G with a comfortable 2-0 victory over Namibia in Douala.

Meanwhile, Newcastle United striker Yoane Wissa opened the scoring as DR Congo continued their perfect start with a 3-1 triumph over Sierra Leone in Kinshasa.

The Leopards are on nine points at the top of Group E, five points ahead of Zimbabwe and Equatorial Guinea after those two sides drew 0-0.

Nigeria were handed a boost after Group L leaders Guinea-Bissau could only manage a 1-1 draw in their away tie against Madagascar in neutral Morocco.

The Super Eagles trail Guinea-Bissau by four points ahead of their home game against Tanzania on Friday (16:00 GMT).

Tanzania are assured of a place at Afcon 2027 as tournament co-hosts, with the other three sides battling for one qualification spot.

And Benin bolstered their bid to reach back-to-back finals with a 4-1 win over Central African Republic.

Gernot Rohr's Cheetahs lead Group F by three points from Burkina Faso, who entertain Mauritania on Friday.

In Group D, another section with just one spot available, Guinea moved level on points with table-toppers South Africa after seeing off Eritrea 2-1 in Conakry.

"It's official between them," a source told E! News in January 2022, with a second insider adding, "They are both artistic and creative, so they bond over being musicians."

In 2025, the couple confirmed their engagement.

The “Beautiful Soul” singer and the Step Up Revolution actress got engaged in 2019 after seven years of dating, tying the knot in Carmel, Calif., on Oct. 23, 2021.

The romance also served as inspiration for much of McCartney’s new music, telling E! News in 2021, “I feel like life sort of needs to happen between each record to be able to write something special and new.”

“For me in this case, obviously, a lot of it was my relationship with Katie,” he added, “and how that growth has affected me and affected my writing."

The couple welcomed son Archer in May 2025 and announced in October 2026 they were expecting their second baby together.

The "Body on Me" collaborators dated on and off between 2003 and 2013, then rekindled their romance in 2023. They tied the knot in a private December 2023 wedding ceremony, with Ashanti giving birth to the couple's first baby in July 2024.

The pair tied the knot in December 2018 and later welcomed daughter Malti Marie in January 2022.

"Family is a big part of my life. It's always been a part of my dreams," Chopra  told E! News' Daily Pop in January 2021, with Nick adding the next month, "We're blessed to have each other and have a full heart for the future."

The Grammy winner saw sparks fly with the Kansas City Chiefs football player during the cruel summer of 2023.

“This all started when Travis very adorably put me on blast on his podcast, which I thought was metal as hell,” she told TIME in December 2023. “We started hanging out right after that. So we actually had a significant amount of time that no one knew, which I’m grateful for, because we got to get to know each other. By the time I went to that first game, we were a couple. I think some people think that they saw our first date at that game? We would never be psychotic enough to hard launch a first date.”

But there was no denying the alchemy between this duo.

In August 2025, Kelce proposed to the "Enchanted" singer in his backyard and the pair officially tied the knot in July 2026.

The One Direction alum sparked dating rumors with the Blink Twice director in September 2025 after stepping out several times in New York. By April 2026, the pair began sparking engagement rumors due to Kravitz stepping out with a big ring on that finger.

And while neither Styles, nor Kravitz confirmed their romance, the High Fidelity alum shared a bit of insight into their high profile romance.

“I’m aware it’s happening,” she told British Vogue of the interest in the pair's relationship in June 2026. “I’m aware when it’s happening, like when there are eight people outside my house, that’s super uncomfortable. I’m aware of all the ingredients that create the thing we’re talking about. But that doesn’t mean you’re necessarily OK with it.”

The music legends tied the knot on April 4, 2008 and went on to welcome daughter Blue Ivy on January 7, 2012 and twins Rumi and Sir on June 13, 2017.

"I was 20 years old when we first started dating," Beyoncé told Jay-Z on his birthday in 2006. "You taught me how to be a woman. You taught me how to live. You taught me how to be a friend. You've given me so much in life."

The singer said hello to a new romance when she reconnected with the sports agent in 2021. Later that year, she praised him as "hilarious" and "very smart" during her CBS special, noting, "It's quite incredible watching him do what he does and just the easiness of it and very smooth."

As Adele told The Hollywood Reporter in December 2023, "Rich and I have always known everything about each other since the day we got together."

After news broke of Ariana's split with husband Dalton Gomez in July 2023, she said "thank u, next" and started a relationship with her Wicked costar, who officially filed for divorce from his wife Lilly Jay in September 2023.

By 2026, though, it appeared the duo had gone their separate ways—with Grande rekindling a romance with Ricky Alvarez.

The couple met while working on her 2022 single "Substance" and she debuted her romance with the "Too Easy" artist in August 2022.

They got engaged in December 2023 and made it official in May 2025.

"We worked really well together and we're also just super in love," the Disney alum said on The Jennifer Hudson Show shortly after her engagement. "It's amazing to find someone that you just laugh with and that you get to make music with."

They found love after first meeting over a decade ago. The singers performed "Cockiness" at the 2012 MTV Video Music Awards and grew closer over the years. Things seemed to turn romantic by 2018, when they cozied up at a Louis Vuitton fashion show.

The couple welcomed son RZA in May 2022 and baby boy Riot Rose in August 2023, followed by daughter Rocki Irish in September 2025.

Her love didn't cost a thing—except 20 years' wait. Though they originally got engaged in November 2002, Affleck and Lopez ultimately broke up and spent years apart. Their rekindled romance took off, with a second engagement in April 2022 and tied the knot just three months later.

However, the greatest love story never told ended in August 2024, when Lopez filed for divorce. Their divorce was settled in January 2025.

Following the whirlwind, Lopez shared a glimpse into how she was feeling in a cryptic Instagram post saying, "Oh, it was a summer."

#868. Young duo at heart of Nations League's meanest defence

Northern Ireland play Ukraine in Belfast on Saturday before travelling to Budapest to face Hungary on Tuesday

Across his two spells as Northern Ireland boss, Michael O'Neill has been blessed with no shortage of centre-back talent.

Jonny Evans, Aaron Hughes, Gareth McAuley and Craig Cathcart were mainstays of his first stint in charge - so much so that, in some of the biggest games of O'Neill's managerial career at Euro 2016, the quartet all started across a flat back-four.

Since returning to the job four years ago, O'Neill has switched to three at the back, with Sunderland duo Trai Hume and Dan Ballard providing an injection of Premier League quality in what remains a side largely drawn from the Championship and League One.

But with Hume, something of a Swiss army knife in the squad, covering the injured Conor Bradley on the right flank and even starting in centre midfield against Ukraine last month, and Ballard presently nursing an injured hamstring, change has been required through this Nations League campaign.

Despite those forced alterations in defence, the side go into their concluding Group B2 fixtures against Ukraine and Hungary top of their pool and the only side at any level of the competition yet to concede a goal.

At the heart of their defensive efforts have been Ruairi McConville and Tom Atcheson, two young centre-backs already described by their international manager as having "no ceiling".

Birthdays and broken lamps - at home with the Charles brothers

NI can draw on strong club form in key window

At 21-years-old, Norwich City's McConville is the more senior of the pair.

Having been given his debut off the bench at home to Belarus two years ago this week, among the former Brighton man's early international assignments was trying to keep a rampant Alexander Isak in check during a 5-1 defeat by Sweden.

In the short time since he has looked an increasingly commanding figure, leading this Nations League group in clearances made with both head and boot.

"It would be unbelievable to keep that record for these last two games and go the whole of the campaign," he said of what is Northern Ireland's longest run without conceding a goal since 2017.

McConville notes that the streak is a team effort and product of collective work-rate, rather than just the defensive three alone.

"We're a team that works hard, a team that doesn't want to give anything up.

"We're confident in ourselves and we know that we're a good side."

It is McConville who has taken on the Ballard role in the middle of the defence for the past three games, with Atcheson on the right and Oxford United's Ciaron Brown, himself superb through the campaign so far, playing from the left.

On the developing understanding between an emerging unit, McConville added: "We're enjoying playing together.

"It's still early days together and we have to keep taking it game by game and doing what the gaffer tells us and the work on the training pitch.

"We don't have much time together when we're here [in international camp] so it's important to do all we can."

Watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two NI from19:15 GMT; Listen on BBC Sounds and BBC Radio Ulster; Watch, listen, live text and clips on BBC Sport app & website

Atcheson's comfort on the ball has been an asset across his six caps

After 16 caps, McConville is a relative veteran compared to Atcheson, who made his international bow in a friendly against Wales in March at a time when he had only four senior club starts to his name at Blackburn Rovers.

The most recent of those had come under O'Neill, then in a short stint as caretaker manager at the Championship club.

Clearly impressed by what he saw from the now 20-year-old at Ewood Park, Atcheson made his first Northern Ireland start against Guinea in June, a game in which he scored the winner with a fabulous flick before later being shown a red card.

Some 428 minutes into his international career, Atcheson is still to experience what it feels like to concede a goal.

The England-born defender feels Ballard "is definitely a big miss" to the side, but believes the squad's understanding of O'Neill's desired system is an asset to those who have starred during the Sunderland man's latest absence.

"I feel like everyone knows what they need to do, everyone knows their job, the details of the formation we play and system," he said.

"That's so key and I think that's why we're so solid defensively.

"It's a team thing, we're set up right, we're very on it all the time and everyone gives their all."

#865. SFA in talks with Boston officials over biennial friendly match

The Tartan Army made a big impression on the city of Boston during the World Cup

BBC Scotland has learned that the SFA is in active discussions aimed at a biennial friendly match being held in Boston.

Scotland played two World Cup matches in the US city during the summer and now the governing body and the state of Massachusetts are in talks aimed at building the bonds made between locals and the Tartan Army, through football.

More discussions are due to take place between the SFA and a delegation of state senators ahead of Scotland's Nations League match against North Macedonia at Hampden on Friday.

It has not yet been decided who will play in the game but BBC Scotland understands it will involve the Scoland national team.

US state senator Paul Feeney has been in the UK this week for talks around energy, but wanted to visit Scotland to build on the bonds made between the Tartan Army and those who partied with them for two weeks in June.

The state of Massachusetts has also passed a bill aimed at strengthening ties with Scotland after an estimated 25,000 fans partied in Boston and surrounding areas.

"We felt that this summer was more than just a football match, more than just, you know, 90 minutes at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough," Feeney said.

"It was a couple of weeks of these relationships being held, and you don't see that often. And I'm glad we got to experience it. And, frankly, we don't want that to end."

He added: "One of the things that we've been active on in Massachusetts today is to kind of take the lessons that we've learned, put together the best practices, and say, ok, we understand that we can't have a World Cup every year, but where we have such a strong connection with people in Scotland, could we do some sort of invitational tournament?

"To have that cultural exchange to kind of prop up economic development, and more than that, just to come together, have a few drinks, and enjoy each other's company."

Scotland fans placed cones on several Boston statues during their time in the city

Feeney said the Massachusetts Senate voted unanimously to support the concept.

"We're trying to work that through the legislature, get it to the finish," he said.

Talks aimed at organising a regular fixture are at an early stage but the SFA is already in advanced negotiations with businesses in Massachusetts about investment in the Scottish game.

"The Tartan Army invaded Massachusetts and I have to say they lit a spark that set off fireworks," Massachusetts Senate president Karen Spilka told BBC Scotland.

"They were sorely missed by so many people when they left.

"I think that by making the effort to come here and meet people and talk about tourism and economic development, we can start talking about things like Tartan Day and maybe having other events going on."

#863. England's Blues brothers - how the Bellinghams helped save Birmingham

Jude Bellingham shared an old photo of him and brother Jobe after England's squad announcement last week

It is six years since Jude Bellingham played his final game for Birmingham City, and three years since younger brother Jobe wore the club's shirt for the last time.

While Jude, 23, is establishing himself as a footballing great at European greats Real Madrid following a spell at Borussia Dortmund, Jobe, 21, is continuing his football education at his brother's former club in Germany after two seasons with Sunderland.

The Stourbridge-born midfielders have moved on with their careers.

Their memories, however, live on at St Andrew's, such was the impact the boyhood Birmingham fans made in the Championship.

On match days supporters stop and pose for photographs in front of Jude's mural outside the ground. Fans still turn up to matches wearing Bellingham shirts.

"They both had a real connection with fans," Craig Courtney, from the Tilton Talk fan podcast, told BBC Sport. "Fans loved the fact they both cared.

"They wore their hearts on their sleeves and helped Birmingham when we were fighting relegation. Even now, Jude and Jobe remember where it all started for them."

The brothers played 70 league and cup games between them for Birmingham after graduating from the academy.

They have never appeared together in a senior match, however, as Jude - who joined Birmingham aged eight - had left by the time Jobe broke into the first team in 2022.

The Bellinghams will become the first brothers to play for England for 19 years if Jobe wins his first cap and appears alongside Jude, a veteran of 60 appearances, in the Nations League game with Croatia at Wembley.

"It will be an incredibly proud moment for Birmingham City if that happens," said Courtney.

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up

Listen: How Jude Bellingham became a global brand

Birmingham supporters have had little to cheer about recently.

It is 15 years since they last appeared in the Premier League, while the 2011 League Cup winners even dipped down to League One recently.

While fierce rivals Aston Villa were playing - and beating - Bayern Munich and Bologna in the Champions League two years ago, Birmingham were losing at Shrewsbury and drawing with Northampton Town.

After 15 games Birmingham sit top of the Championship and there are plans for a new 62,000-capacity stadium in time for 2030-31.

"As a club, we've been right down in the doldrums," added Courtney. "Now we're top of the table and having a new stadium built.

"There is an argument that none of this would have been possible without the fees received for Jude and Jobe."

A mural tribute to Jude Bellingham outside St Andrew's

Jude is the youngest player in Birmingham's history after making his debut aged 16 years and 38 days in 2019.

Clubs across Europe were pursuing him when he signed his first professional contact in 2020 after turning 17 - a deal both he and Birmingham knew would never be fulfilled.

His actions, however, ensured Birmingham would receive a significant transfer fee when he left, and soon afterwards he joined Dortmund for an initial fee of Â£20m during the Covid-19 pandemic.

When he joined Real in 2023, Birmingham received a reported sell-on fee of at least Â£10m., external

"We cannot possibly imagine, without Jude's decision [to sign a contract], where we would be as a club in a pandemic like this," then Birmingham chief executive Xuandong Ren told BBC WM after Jude joined Dortmund.

"He could easily have just looked after himself and not the club, but he chose the best possible way to look after the club."

Jobe became the second youngest player to play for Birmingham when he made his debut in January 2022 aged 16 years and 107 days.

"This was a lad, regardless of who his brother was or what he was achieving, who would do anything to write his own success story," former Birmingham striker Troy Deeney, who played in the game when Jobe made his debut, told the Sun., external

"Everything he has achieved on the pitch, too, has come with an instant comparison to his older brother.

"He never got that one moment to enjoy something without someone, somewhere saying: 'Yeah, but what about Jude?'

"That only added to how strong he was mentally, and anyone who suggests he is where he is because of his last name is talking rubbish."

Deeney added: "What impressed me more than anything he had done on the pitch was his attitude - a hell-bent determination to get to the top and the common sense to take all the right steps along the way."

Jobe played 26 games before Sunderland paid Â£3m for him in 2023, with Birmingham receiving a reported Â£4m sell-on fee when he moved to Dortmund two years later.

Although significantly less than the fees generated by his brother, it was nevertheless welcome revenue.

Jobe Bellingham was given his Birmingham City debut by manager Lee Bowyer in January 2022

Both Jude and Jobe have returned to St Andrew's since their transfers.

Jobe captained England Under-21s to a 2-0 win against the Republic of Ireland at his old ground last November.

Before that match U21s boss Lee Carsley, who managed Jude when he was England interim manager in 2024, praised the brothers for their work ethic and determination to be the best.

Carsley said: "I know how much they love the Blues still and how important the club is to them."

Jude, tipped to be a future England captain, was at St Andrew's in July watching his former club in a pre-season friendly against Barcelona. He even wore a Birmingham shirt while watching from the stands.

Jude wore a Birmingham City shirt when he returned to St Andrew's

When Jude joined Dortmund in 2020 Birmingham retired the 17-year-old's number 22 shirt after 44 appearances.

"That was a gesture of thanks for what Jude had done," said Courtney.

"It might be wishful thinking, but I really believe Jude has unfinished business at Birmingham. I can see a scenario before he retires where he gets an opportunity to wear the number 22 again."

Should the Bellingham brothers play together against Croatia, they will become the first siblings to appear for England since Gary and Phil Neville against Spain in a friendly at Old Trafford in 2007.

It will be an immensely proud moment for their parents, Mark and Denise.

"We've played together for so long in the street and to play with my brother Jobe for England would be the biggest dream of my life," Jude, a Champions League and La Liga winner with Real Madrid, wrote on social media, external in 2024.

"That would mean more than any of the trophies. Nothing would even get close to that... nothing."

BBC reporter John Watson has been finding out why Bellingham is proving so popular with football fans across the world

#862. Michael Carrick was just the latest fall guy for Manchester United’s dysfunctional hierarchy | Jamie Jackson

Disastrous decisions and confused appointments have been a constant theme at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013

For a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking, consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one.

The former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick. Howe was also the favoured candidate of Dan Ashworth, Wilcox’s predecessor as United’s director of football, to follow Erik ten Hag after the Dutchman’s sacking in October 2024. Except Wilcox disagreed and Sir Jim Ratcliffe went with Wilcox’s man, Ruben Amorim, and that December Ashworth departed only five months after joining.

At that juncture Wilcox was the technical director. Now he is United’s highest-ranking football executive, the powerbroker. He was able, apparently with a straight face, to recommend to Ratcliffe that Howe, nearly two years after he rejected him, should become United’s eighth permanent No 1 in the 13 and a half years since Sir Alex Ferguson retired.

If following this is difficult, making sense of it is near impossible. Should London’s West End need a new farce then look no further than the wacky world of Ratcliffe and the football department he leads, which is also headed up by Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and is proving a disjointed, illogical operation.

Yet if this meant Carrick was dealt a treacherous hand, it is also true that he should have played it better. This, after all, is the job of a football coach: to somehow make wine from water – even if the water is murky, and may need purifying first.

José Mourinho, one of Carrick’s predecessors, from May 2016 to December 2018, showed how – to a degree. Mourinho stated famously that leading United to second place in 2017-18 (with 81 points, 19 behind Manchester City) was one of his finest achievements. This from a serial winner who broke the United-Arsenal duopoly of the Premier League to take Chelsea to consecutive crowns (2004-05 and 2005-06), and made history in Italy by guiding Inter to the treble in 2009-10.

Mourinho’s billing of that second place was down to having to negotiate a similar shambles, overseen by Ed Woodward, the then executive vice-chair.

The Portuguese’s opening campaign ended with the Carabao Cup and Europa League collected despite, like Carrick, having to deal with a hierarchy convinced that it knew better than the man it hired as the football expert.

Here we arrive at a fundamental quality Carrick lacked: an ability to be streetwise when really required. For an example of Mourinho’s nous, rewind to a pre-season tour of America when this correspondent was offered an off-the-record sounding about a player he wanted out of the club but the executive did not.

The manager wanted his message out – that this was a player non grata. Machiavellian or pragmatic? A guess says Carrick would never dream of employing a similar tactic to achieve the best result for the team. But why not? Mourinho wanted a bad egg gone before the dressing room was stunk out and on-field prospects undermined.

Carrick, in his last month, encountered two of his own malevolents: Lisandro Martínez, a de facto captain who dared to criticise Wilcox’s recruitment after the 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid; and Bruno Fernandes, Carrick’s official leader, who betrayed his manager by questioning his tactics after the 4-1 humiliation at Como.

Each crossed a line and were emblematic of a chaotic changing room, a major factor in the dismal run of three wins from 15 games this season, including elimination from the Carabao Cup, and the league return of eight points from 10 matches that has United in the relegation zone.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Fernandes, Martínez and a club run like a banana republic are the next man’s problem, just as Mourinho inherited from Louis van Gaal, who was sacked the day after winning the 2016 FA Cup, the faults at boardroom level embodied by Woodward.

Here we see the recurring problem at United: a new gun is hired and is bequeathed a sorry mess that is impossible to clean up because there is no true will to eradicate it. Why? Because the only real reset of culture would be for Ratcliffe, who owns 29.4%, Wilcox, Berrada and the Glazer family, whose ownership since 2005 has left the club about £1.2bn in debt, to accept they are the problem and depart.

Carrick is a good guy whose adoration of United was returned to him by the support, underlined by the reception he got from the Stretford End after the 3-0 humbling by Bournemouth last month. Yet being a decent man and head coach was not enough.

In elite sport the fine margins are often trumpeted as the difference between triumph and failure. Last season, from mid-January, Carrick worked these his way as Manchester City, Arsenal, Liverpool and Chelsea were defeated and United lost only two of his 17 games as interim head coach.

This season, though, the fall-off was startling – and Carrick was found wanting. Who knows what might have occurred if United were the “best-in-class” organisation Ratcliffe insisted they would be under him. As with the muddled thinking regarding Howe, “worst in class” may be a more apt characterisation.

The agonising, overlong process to decide Carrick should be sacked was the latest illustration. On Monday evening the Guardian broke the news that Wilcox and Berrada would recommend to Ratcliffe that Carrick should be removed. Yet days passed during which Carrick still took training and it emerged the deal for Pochettino was being finalised. A proper functioning organisation would have acted more swiftly and with more style.

This is what the next manager has to grapple with. He may succeed. But the odds are stacked against it owing to the deep structural faults that undermine the modern Manchester United.

Understanding the scale of a problem can be the first step to finding solutions. Wildlife is traded around the world, by legal or illegal means, and gaining information about the extent of this trade offers a way to guide strategies for conservation work that helps to prevent biodiversity loss.
